Results Soil parameters (pH, soil water content, temperature, and total C and N contents) varied significantly between sites and revealed pH and C: N ratio as key drivers modulated by vegetation cover, highlighting its indirect role in shaping soil environments. Microbial community composition differed significantly across sites, and functional gene profiles mirrored taxonomic patterns, indicating strong coupling between community structure and functional gene potential, with reduced functional redundancy. Microbial abundance increased with vegetation cover, whereas taxonomic and functional gene diversity plateaued at intermediate vegetation cover, suggesting that the presence of vegetation primarily enhances microbial abundance rather than diversity. Vegetated soils exhibited lower, pH and C: N ratio, shaping a more abundant microbial community with more specialist members and higher C cycling gene potential. papers.title: INR-MHM: an implicit neural representation framework for continuous hemispherical modeling of GNSS multipath errors
papers.summary: Abstract Multipath error is one of the primary factors limiting high-precision Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) positioning, particularly in complex urban canyon environments. Conventional GNSS Multipath Hemispherical Map (MHM) methods rely on discrete spatial grids, which limit spatial resolution and lack the capability to jointly represent multi-system and multi-frequency observations within a unified framework. Deep learning-based methods can provide continuous fitting of multipath errors. However, standard neural networks exhibit spectral bias, which can limit their ability to represent high-frequency spatial variations caused by severe obstructions and strong reflections. To address these challenges, this study proposes an implicit neural representation framework, termed INR-MHM, for continuous modeling of multipath errors for multi-system and multi-frequency GNSS. The proposed method reformulates the discrete multipath field into a continuous coordinate-based function. Specifically, this model introduces a multi-scale Fourier spatial encoding technique to map low-dimensional spatial coordinates into a high-frequency feature space, thereby mitigating the spectral bias of neural networks. Simultaneously, a context-gated feature fusion mechanism is designed to dynamically integrate multidimensional attributes, such as spatial geometry, signal frequency, and signal quality. Finally, a lightweight nonlinear regression head maps the fused representation to the estimated Single-Differenced (SD) carrier-phase multipath correction. papers.title: State as the Ultimate Landlord? Shifting Social Contract, Rights and Expectations in the Republic of Georgia
papers.summary: Who takes responsibility for a house damaged by an environmental disaster? After a deadly landslide in the western highlands of Georgia in 1989, the Soviet state-initiated resettlement and housing provision for disaster-affected people, whose houses were destroyed in the landslide. While the disaster-affected population was temporarily resettled in the empty houses left by the Greek communities in the southern part of Georgia, the question of state housing provision became increasingly ambiguous after 1991. This paper examines the shift in the post-socialist social contract, entailing a rearrangement of rights and expectations between the state and the citizen, as well as among citizens. Building on historical ethnography of changing property regimes, state–citizen relations, and privatization vis-à-vis environmental disasters, the paper explores the moral engagement and informal property regime that emerged among people as a response to the unreliable landlord state.

This report presents an analysis of the Tracy Arm tsunami along with a review of several major landslides and associated tsunamis that occurred on the coasts of British Columbia and southeastern Alaska. Major focus is on three of the most destructive events: (1) the Kwalate historical event (~1570 AD); (2) the 1958 Lituya Bay event; and (3) the 2015 Taan Fjord event. The scale, physical mechanisms and properties of these three landslides and tsunamis are very similar to those generated by the 2025 Tracy Arm failure. For this study, we examined all available information on the 2025 Tracy Arm event, including photos, videos and satellite imagery. We also examined data from six NOAA tide gauges located in the vicinity of the slide and from six Canadian Hydrographic Survey tide gauges located in northern British Columbia. A tsunami wave was evident in only one station, Juneau, the closest to the landslide source area. The first tsunami wave arrived at Juneau at 14:12 UTC, i.e., 46 min after the landslide. papers.title: Spatial dynamic rainfall thresholds for landslide in the Aburrá Valley, Colombia
papers.summary: Abstract. Rainfall-triggered landslides are frequent in the Aburrá Valley, a densely populated Andean valley in Colombia, where warnings must tell where as well as when slopes become critical. We derived rainfall thresholds for each slope unit from 492 dated landslides (2011–2025), four terrain variables, rainfall and the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phase. Non-landslide observations were drawn under three designs that share the landslide's slope unit, its date, or neither, each resampled 100 times. For each design we compared logistic regression, generalized additive models and random forests. A one-day window best described the trigger; for antecedent rainfall, 30 days was chosen among several equivalent windows. Median areas under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve ranged from 0.955 to 0.988. The algorithms differed little within a design, whereas the design changed which predictors carried the signal. Three cut-offs on the ROC curve of the additive model define four alert levels, whose rainfall thresholds change with land cover, slope, soil, ENSO phase and antecedent rainfall. In the larger of two landslide events of 2025 kept out of training, 78 % of the evaluated slope units with landslides reached High or Very high before the report, while 11 % of the valley did.

papers.title: Experimental Investigation of Buried Pipeline Response and Failure Under Lateral Landslide Loading
papers.summary: Buried oil and gas pipelines crossing landslide-prone terrain are vulnerable to large ground deformation, yet their progressive pipe–soil interaction and failure behavior remain insufficiently characterized experimentally. This study investigates the mechanical response and failure of a shallow-buried steel pipeline subjected to lateral landslide loading using large-scale physical model tests. The experiment comprised sequential slope inclination adjustments in 5° increments, followed by displacement-controlled loading at a slope inclination of 30°, while pipeline axial strain, surrounding soil pressure, and deflection were monitored. The results show that increasing slope inclination intensified strain concentration near the pipeline midspan. During displacement loading, the tensile strain peaked at approximately 8100 με at a landslide displacement of 50 mm, whereas the compressive strain reached approximately −12,400 με at 58 mm. Frontal soil pressure peaked earlier, at approximately 44–45 kPa near 46 mm displacement, indicating that peak soil resistance preceded pipeline instability. Local buckling subsequently developed near the pipeline midspan, accompanied by approximately symmetric beam-like global bending. Comparisons with a PSI soil-spring model and a three-dimensional solid-contact finite-element model showed reasonable agreement during the pre-buckling response but substantial underestimation of strain after local buckling, with predicted values less than half the measured magnitude. These findings clarify the transition from soil-resistance-controlled deformation to localized structural instability and provide experimental evidence for evaluating buried pipelines subjected to landslide-induced ground deformation.

papers.title: Causal-stage attribution for debris-flow cascades in changing mountain regions
papers.summary: Debris-flow inventories usually record where and when events occur but often compress source initiation, transformation and runout into one whole-event label. This is problematic in high mountains, where rainfall, melt, ground-ice thaw, rock–ice failure, lake release and channel entrainment can occupy different causal roles within a single cascade. We propose an evidence-graded six-stage attribution architecture that records conditioning context, dynamic preconditioning, proximate initiator, release mechanism, transformation and routing/runout separately. Water source and external forcing are treated as attributes rather than stages, and each stage retains its evidence basis, corroboration, plausible alternatives and unresolved status. The framework is designed to reduce prediction-time data leakage, align monitoring signals with the decisions they can support, and distinguish background climate influence from event-scale initiation. We outline benchmark inventories and prospective tests against binary baselines to determine when stage-resolved attribution improves interpretability, transferability, calibration or forecast updating.

papers.source: RESEARCH JOURNAL OF PURE SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
papers.summary: This study investigates soil erodibility in three Local Government Areas (LGAs) within Anambra State, Nigeria—Ekwusigo, Ihiala, and Ogbaru—situated in the lower Niger River Basin prone to frequent and severe flooding. The aim is to assess geological and soil characteristics influencing landslide susceptibility. The methodology involves identifying and characterizing soil types, calculating the Soil Erodibility Factor (K) using empirical formulas, and mapping erosion susceptibility. Data from the Soil Map of the World (version 3.6) were used, corrected for accuracy, and integrated into geographic projections. Analysis included William’s equation to calculate K factors based on soil properties such as sand, silt, clay, and organic matter content. Results highlight diverse geological formations: Ameki Group (34.24%), Benin Formation (0.26%), Ogwashi-Asaba Formation (1.59%), River Niger (1.86%), Sands, Gravels, and Clay (42.36%), and Sombreiro Warri Deltaic Plain (19.69%). Soil types identified include Dystric Nitosols (K = 0.0178) covering 449.11 km² and Gleysols (K = 0.0189) covering 283.95 km², each exhibiting unique erosion susceptibilities. Gleysols are characterized by poor drainage and high-water retention, posing higher landslide risks during heavy rainfall compared to Dystric Nitosols. The correlation between K factors and hydrological data, showing Gleysols as more vulnerable to landslides in wet conditions. Recommendations include targeted erosion control measures like terracing, vegetative buffers, and improved drainage systems for high-risk zones. Maintaining vegetative cover and implementing sustainable land management practices are crucial for mitigating erosion and landslide risks. This study provides a detailed understanding of geological and soil factors affecting landslide susceptibility in Anambra State. Linking a RUSLE-derived erosion proxy to clustered shallow landslides triggered by extreme rainfall: evidence from Typhoon Doksuri in Laishui County, Northern China
papers.summary: Extreme rainfall can trigger widespread shallow landsliding, yet accumulated rainfall alone does not adequately explain its spatial concentration. We examined 15,622 landslides mapped following Typhoon Doksuri in Laishui County, northern China, of which 15,387 were retained for modelling. A RUSLE-derived event erosion proxy (EEP) was constructed by combining 10-day accumulated rainfall, soil erodibility, slope length and steepness, and land-cover factors. Its log-transformed form, EEP′ = ln (EEP + 1), showed a clearer positive association with landslide number density and area percentage than accumulated rainfall alone. Among four logistic regression models, the model incorporating both rainfall and EEP′ alongside conventional conditioning factors achieved the best discrimination and fit (five-fold AUC = 0.7736; AIC = 33,938.81). Spatial-block validation yielded the same model ranking, with the combined model achieving the highest AUC (0.7489). Component-wise comparisons indicated additional improvement in model fit, while random forest analysis identified EEP′ as an influential predictor. These findings support the use of EEP′ as a readily derived, interpretable indicator for characterising spatial differences in shallow-landslide occurrence and supporting regional screening after extreme rainfall. Its broader applicability remains to be tested across other events and regions.

papers.title: Solid-like to Flow-like Transition in Granite Residual Soil Based on Ring-Shear Tests and Empirical Parameterization
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides in granite residual soils commonly undergo a rapid transition from relatively blocky sliding to highly mobile flow. This transition is influenced by multiple factors, including soil composition, particle-size distribution and particle rearrangement, among which normal stress and shear velocity are two key mechanical variables. To investigate their effects, a series of ring-shear tests was conducted on remolded granite residual soil under applied normal stresses of 100, 150, and 200 kPa and shear velocities ranging from 0.5 to 10,000 mm/min. The tests were designed to characterize the evolution of peak and steady-state shear resistance over a wide velocity range and to establish an empirical representation of the combined effects of shear velocity and normal stress on the frictional response. The results show that the peak shear resistance exhibits an overall rate-strengthening trend, with increases of 69.1%, 38.7%, and 37.6% under normal stresses of 100, 150, and 200 kPa, respectively, from the lowest to the highest tested velocity. In contrast, the steady-state shear resistance exhibits non-monotonic and normal-stress-dependent variations, with the minimum measured resistance occurring at different velocities under the three normal-stress conditions. Post-shear observations further reveal progressive localization and restructuring of the main shear band with increasing velocity, consistent with a transition from predominantly friction-dominated shearing toward increasingly flow-like deformation. Based on the experimental results, an apparent friction coefficient was defined using the steady-state shear resistance and the applied total normal stress. papers.title: Spatio‐Temporal Modelling of Extreme Rainfall Occurrence in Brazil
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Extreme rainfall events are major hydroclimatic hazards in Brazil, causing floods, landslides, infrastructure damage, and agricultural losses across distinct climatic regions. This study develops a Bayesian spatio‐temporal Log‐Gaussian Cox Process (LGCP) framework to model the occurrence of extreme precipitation using CHIRPS daily rainfall data. The results reveal clear differences between moderate‐extreme and ultra‐extreme rainfall regimes. Lower thresholds are strongly influenced by seasonal forcing associated with the South American Monsoon System, whereas the most severe events exhibit stronger temporal dependence, episodic clustering, and more localized spatial organization, indicating increasingly persistent spatio‐temporal structures in the latent risk field as precipitation intensity increases. Regional decompositions further show substantial heterogeneity in trends, seasonality, and persistence across Brazil, reflecting the influence of distinct hydroclimatic regimes and atmospheric processes. The estimated latent spatial fields identify persistent high‐risk corridors over the Amazon basin, southeastern coastal Brazil, and southern subtropical regions. Overall, the findings suggest that extreme rainfall occurrence in Brazil is governed by multiple interacting regional processes whose persistence and spatial organization may evolve under climate variability and climate change.

papers.title: GLOF and LDOF Cascade Pathogen Ecology: The Invisible Bridge from Bamboo to Alpine Flora as High-Altitude Bioindicators for One Health
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Abstract Catastrophic Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) and Landslide Dam Outburst Floods (LDOFs) in the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) are traditionally evaluated as physical geohazards or acute waterborne disease triggers (Adhikari, 2026d; Pal et al., 2024). However, these cascades also act as high-velocity ecological conveyors that mobilise dormant cryospheric microorganisms, soil-borne pathogens, and heavy metals across steep altitudinal gradients. Building upon longitudinal disaster timelines (2012–2026) demonstrating that alpine containment failures cluster within the nocturnal "Dawn Cascade" (01:30–09:15 local time) and exploit eight systemic monitoring blind spots (Adhikari, 2026a, 2026b), this paper synthesises the pathogen ecology of GLOF-LDOF cascades within a One Health framework. We propose an altitudinal botanical surveillance continuum—an "invisible bridge"—linking mid-hill riparian bamboo groves (Dendrocalamus and Bambusa spp.) with high-altitude alpine flora (Rhododendron, Kobresia, and cushion-forming species). While shallow-rooted bamboo acts as a hydro-mechanical and biological sentinel for subsurface seepage, faecal-pathogen loading, and toxic runoff in lower valleys (Adhikari, 2026c; Tang et al., 2024), alpine cushion plants and sedges serve as early-warning bioindicators of permafrost-thaw microbial reactivation and heavy-metal leaching at the cryospheric fringe. Integrating botanical stress diagnostics with community-based One Health triage provides a low-cost, zero-power bio-surveillance network aligned with United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs 3, 11, 13, and 15) (United Nations University [UNU], 2025; Zommers & MacDonald, 2014).

papers.title: Applicability of regional frequency analysis on TRMM-based average recurrence interval for extreme rainfall monitoring in the Philippines
papers.summary: Given the Philippines’ susceptibility to hydrometeorological hazards associated with extreme rainfall, a reliable and accurate monitoring system is critical for protecting lives and property. However, current extreme rainfall monitoring tools often rely on static rainfall thresholds applied uniformly across all areas, failing to account for regional variability. Additionally, challenges such as limited spatial coverage and short time periods of data further complicate effective monitoring of these events. This study presents a tool for detecting potential extreme rainfall events using average recurrence interval (ARI) and regional frequency analysis (RFA) approaches on TRMM 3B42 data from 1998 to 2015. Through RFA, robust, time-dependent, and location-specific ARI statistics are derived to quantify the rarity of observed or forecast rainfall. Following Hosking and Wallis (1997), rainfall data were first grouped into homogeneous regions, after which precipitation quantiles for various ARIs were estimated. Results indicate that RFA-based estimates produce lower root-mean-square error (RMSE) than traditional frequency analysis, demonstrating improved reliability. Application to three historical extreme rainfall events of varying intensity and impact shows that ARI maps broadly capture areas affected by heavy precipitation, which led to flooding and landslides. Despite these strengths, limitations remain. ARI estimates are constrained by the relatively short TRMM 3B42 record, introducing uncertainty at higher return periods. Additionally, the use of daily rainfall totals limits detection of short-duration extremes (e.g., 3- or 6-hour events). Nevertheless, the approach offers a valuable framework for high-resolution monitoring of extreme rainfall across the country.

papers.title: Sustainable Transport Infrastructure: Climate Adaptation Through Nature-Based Solutions. A Cost-Effective Resilient Approach
papers.summary: Abstract Climate change poses growing risks to linear transport infrastructure (LTI) including floods, landslides and other climate-related hazards, causing significant infrastructure damage and economic losses. Within this context, Nature-based Solutions (NbS) are cost-effective adaptive alternatives providing synergic benefits to infrastructure, society, and the planet. NbS can reduce carbon footprint and mainstream biodiversity within LTI contributing to transport operators’ sustainability reporting. Furthermore, they are adaptive and multifunctional, allowing to better deal with the uncertainties of climate change projections and scenarios. However, the current lack of standards, harmonized guidance, and indicators are among the main barriers for upscaling their implementation in the sector. The EU-RAIL SYMBIOSIS (SYstemic Mobilisation for Joint Biodiversity and Infrastructure) project aims to overcome these barriers by developing i) a harmonized methodology to prioritise NbS for climate resilient infrastructure, and ii) guidelines to reinforce Blue and Green Infrastructure on transport and energy networks. Integrating this operational tool into the LTI digital environment (i.e.: Digital Twins) will develop a Decision Support System providing indicators enabling infrastructure managers, policy and decision-makers to identify the best solution according to their specific needs. Furthermore, this integration will permit real-time data collection enabling a continuous improvement process contributing to achieving sustainable and resilient transport networks.

papers.summary: Informal settlements emerge in contexts of rapid urbanisation, rural-to-urban migration, socioeconomic inequality, and environmental and political vulnerabilities and are characterised by spatial segregation, inadequate infrastructure, and limited access to services.Addressing these challenges requires innovative approaches that go beyond conventional urban planning, emphasising strategies that integrate ecological, social, and cultural dimensions of the built environment.This paper explores regenerative design strategies for built environments and urban voids within informal settlements, with a particular attention to contexts marked by high social and ecological vulnerability.Drawing on a case study conducted in a hillside informal settlement in Cali, Colombia, the papers.title: Understanding landslides through case studies
Strategic Resilience in Rail Infrastructure: Lessons from International Resilience Initiatives
papers.summary: Abstract Climate change is escalating extreme weather, profoundly challenging global railways. UIC’s RERA (Resilient Railways) initiative addresses these threats through two reports: “Resilient Railways facing High Temperatures” and “Resilient Railways facing Heavy Rains”. While high temperatures can cause track buckling and heavy rainfall can lead to landslides, both disrupt services and compromise safety. RERA provides shareable lessons and a unified assessment methodology written by infrastructure managers. This paper examines the RERA frameworks, drawing insights from climate impact analysis and vulnerability assessments. It highlights adaptive solutions implemented by member organisations, demonstrating how harmonized approaches safeguard operations. The paper explores the role of multi-modal integration and knowledge sharing in building resilience. By embedding climate projections into planning, railways can transition from reactive to resilient systems, supporting sustainable mobility in a volatile climate.

papers.title: Resolved CFD-DEM Investigation of the Effect of Particle Shape on Clogging Behavior
papers.summary: Abstract Particle clogging in porous media under fluid-driven conditions plays a critical role in various geohazards, including contaminant transport, riverbank collapse, and landslide initiation. However, the influence of particle shape on clogging behavior remains underexplored. This study utilizes a fully resolved computational fluid dynamics–discrete-element method (CFD-DEM) to simulate particle clogging in a truncated conical pore, systematically varying the aspect ratio (AR) of particles from 1.0 to 2.0. A comprehensive analysis is performed to evaluate the impact of particle shape on the characteristics of particle clogging. The results reveal that ellipsoidal particles exhibit continuous fluid-induced rotation, and the major axis tends to align with the flow direction, which significantly reduces the clogging probability at a higher AR. Distinct clogging structures are observed: a dome with parallel-aligned particles usually forms when the fluid velocity is low, while a dome with rotated and interlocked particles and a single arch with parallel-aligned particles become dominant as the velocity increases. A strong negative correlation between average particle velocity and fluid pressure drop is observed across all particle shapes, suggesting that pressure drop can serve as a robust indicator of clogging dynamics. Moreover, higher fluid velocities and larger constriction diameters reduce clogging probability and promote easier particle escape.

papers.title: Information-theoretic modeling of landslide susceptibility using mostly categorical spatial data
papers.summary: Abstract. Landslide susceptibility mapping with machine learning should make full use of inherently informative categorical layers such as lithology, soil type, and land use, yet these variables usually enter models in a diminished, encoded form. Reconstructability Analysis (RA), an information-theoretic method based on Shannon entropy, uses categorical data directly and produces transparent, interpretable models. We applied RA to two contiguous Oregon Coast Range (USA) watersheds (3,500 km²) rated Very High Risk for landslides by the Federal Emergency Management Agency, using ~9,000 landslide deposits mapped mostly from LiDAR by the Oregon Department of Geology and Mineral Industries (DOGAMI), with DOGAMI lithology, Soil Survey, and National Land Cover Database layers; terrain variables were discretized into optimized bins. Variable importance analysis led to stratification into volcanic and sedimentary lithologies, with landslide rates of 44 % and 60 %. The best RA models reached 75 % (volcanic) and 71 % (sedimentary) test accuracy, nearly as good as Random Forest, while remaining interpretable in terms of named soil, landform, and rock units. Their probability tables give landslide likelihood for specific combinations of landform, geology, and elevation; in the sedimentary stratum, two andic soil subgroups emerged as most landslide-prone, consistent with high water retention. The tables are provided as a supplement.

papers.title: Towards multi-hazard assessment: a score-based framework for screening and ranking Italian municipalities
papers.summary: Identifying natural hazard hotspots is essential for disaster risk reduction, yet comparing and aggregating heterogeneous hazards remains challenging due to differences in metrics, spatial-temporal scales, and data availability. This study proposes a transparent, index-based framework for ranking single and multiple natural hazards and identifying multi-hazard hotspots at national and sub-national scales without relying on data-intensive risk modelling. Single-hazard scores are derived by normalising open-source hazard indicators, while multi-hazard scores are obtained by aggregating the individual hazard scores. The framework is applied in Italy as a municipal-scale screening tool for single and multi-hazard hotspot identification considering six natural hazards: earthquakes, floods, landslides, tsunamis, heatwaves, and heavy rainfall. Results show strong differences in the spatial distribution of the considered hazards, with localised hazards such as floods and landslides exhibiting highly skewed distributions, while heatwaves and heavy rainfall display broader territorial diffusion. The highest all-hazard multi-hazard scores are predominantly observed in the Calabria region, where medium-to-high hazard scores simultaneously occur across all considered hazards. The proposed approach provides a scalable and flexible foundation for supporting disaster risk reduction and results can be easily integrated with exposure and vulnerability data to inform more comprehensive risk assessments, particularly in data-constrained contexts.

papers.title: Root Characteristics and Reinforcement Properties of Widely Spaced Native and Poplar Trees in Auckland Hill Country
papers.source: New Zealand Journal of Agricultural Research
papers.summary: Widely spaced trees are commonly established in New Zealand hill country to mitigate shallow landslide erosion. Studies have quantified the root distribution and mechanical properties of poplar in hill country, but comparable data for mature, widely spaced (10–25 m) natives is lacking. This first‐of‐its‐kind study quantifies the root distribution and mechanical properties (tensile strength and displacement at failure) of widely spaced poplar ( Populus deltoides × nigra , Euramericana hybrid), kānuka ( Kunzea ericoides ) and tōtara ( Podocarpus totara ) in two Ultic soil types at three sites in the Auckland region. It then integrates these measurements to compare root reinforcement of each species. The results show that tōtara had the greatest number of roots, dominated by fine roots (91%), but had reduced root reinforcement compared to poplar and kānuka due to the low tensile strength of its roots. Kānuka had fewer coarse roots than poplar, but its strong root mechanical properties led to similar lateral root reinforcement. These results provide additional evidence that root reinforcement for slope stabilisation is the result of the combined effect of both root system architecture and mechanical properties. The calculated and upscaled lateral root reinforcement for both clay soil types of kānuka and poplar showed greater values than tōtara within 0–4 m distance from the trunk, but all species converged to similar values at a >7 m distance. These results indicate that natives can provide similar root reinforcement to Euramericana hybrid poplar, meaning they could offer distinct advantages in reducing shallow landslides due to their greater longevity and the reduced need for replacement (120+ years of lifespan compared to 40–50 years for poplar).

papers.title: An Energy-Variational Model for Buried Pipelines under Mining-Induced Ground Movement Considering Pipe Yielding and Pipe-Soil Interface Slip
papers.summary: Abstract In coal-natural gas resource overlap areas, coal seam extraction induces non-uniform ground movements, which in turn cause axial tensile-compressive deformation and potential plastic failure in buried gas pipelines. Existing models based on the linear-elastic pipe assumption are unable to adequately characterize the coupled evolution of pipe-soil interfacial slip, energy transfer, and material yielding. In this study, based on the principle of minimum potential energy, energy-variational governing equations were established by simultaneously considering pipe yielding and interfacial slip states. A nonlinear solution procedure was developed using finite-difference discretization, incremental loading, active-set identification, damped Newton iteration, and Armijo line search, enabling the synchronous updating of pipe yielding states and pipe-soil friction states. Taking a gas pipeline in a coal mining area in Shanxi Province, China, as an engineering case study, the evolution of pipeline displacement, axial stress, and strain energy under different mining stages and limiting frictional resistance conditions was investigated. The results show that increasing the limiting frictional resistance enhances the transfer of mining-induced ground displacement to the pipeline and promotes the axial propagation of the pipe yielding zone. In particular, the compressed pipe section near the subsidence center constitutes the critical zone governing the risk of pipeline stress failure. A strain-energy reserve index based on the critical yield strain energy was proposed, which distinguishes elastic pipe segments from potential yielding zones. This index provides a basis for graded risk assessment and early warning of pipelines in mining areas. Validation against a three-directional soil-spring finite element model and existing models demonstrates that the proposed model can accurately predict the mechanical response of pipelines throughout the entire mining process. papers.title: Assessment of Numerical Modelling Approaches for the Analysis of Buried Steel Pipelines Subjected to Landslides
papers.source: ERA: Education and Research Archive (University of Alberta)
papers.summary: Buried steel pipelines play an important role in energy transportation systems by delivering essential resources, such as oil and gas, across vast distances. Major transmission pipelines often traverse regions prone to geohazards such as landslides and are therefore vulnerable to the effects of permanent ground displacements (PGDs). When subjected to landslide induced PGDs, pipelines are likely to develop significant longitudinal strains, leading to potential pipeline failure and far-reaching consequences across the environment, economy, and surrounding communities. To analyze the response of pipelines subjected to PGDs, researchers have developed multiple numerical approaches, ranging in fidelity from simplistic beam-spring models to advanced continuum models. Due to its computational efficiency, industrial practice commonly relies on a subset of beam-spring models, referred to as PSI-Pipe models, for the analysis of pipe-soil interactions. This approach employs pipe elements, which are based on Timoshenko beam theory, to represent the pipeline, whereas interactions between the pipeline and surrounding soil are modelled using pipe-soil interaction (PSI) elements. While PSI-Pipe models are commonly used in industry on project-specific cases for tasks such as pipeline design and integrity-based risk assessments, there is currently no guidance within the literature on how key pipeline design parameters influence pipeline response under landslide loading when modelled using this conventional approach. To address this limitation, a comparative parametric analysis was conducted to understand the influence of pipeline design parameters (pipe grade, diameter, wall thickness, soil type, landslide intersection angle, and internal pressure) on pipeline response under landslide induced PGD loading. papers.title: Temporal evaluation and likely causes of rock-slope failure activity in the mid-Pennines, northern England
papers.source: Geografiska Annaler Series A Physical Geography
papers.summary: Coarse rock debris at the surface of 15 relic rock-slope failures (RSFs) in the mid-Pennines of northern England was subjected to Schmidt-hammer exposure-age dating (SHD). The two-point procedure based on old and young control surfaces was used to develop a linear age-calibration curve and equation. The RSFs range in age from 18.11±1.72 to 5.27±1.12 ka but occur in one or other of two broad temporal clusters. One age cluster is in the latter stages of the Late Devensian (Late Weichselian) Stadial (∼18–15 ka), the other is in the Early to Mid-Holocene (11.7–5 ka). There is limited evidence of RSF activity in both the Lateglacial Interstadial (14.7–12.9 ka) and Younger Dryas Stadial (12.9–11.7 ka). Several reasons for these RSFs are considered, but the clustering of ages suggests that certain factors such as glacial unloading/debuttressing, permafrost degradation and/or anthropogenic deforestation are unlikely to have been key trigger mechanisms in all cases. The proximity to major fault systems may account for some of the RSFs, although this would require different faults to have been active at different times, but evidence for post-glacial fault reactivation is limited. Nevertheless, the SHD ages provide geochronological data concerning the timing of significant landshaping events and pose a continuing challenge regarding the determination of relic RSF causation.

papers.title: Social Solidarity in Humanitarian Action during Galodo Disasters in West Sumatra: A Comparative Study
papers.source: International Journal of Community Service Implementation
papers.summary: This study examines patterns of social solidarity in humanitarian action during two galodo-related disaster events in West Sumatra: the widespread floods and landslides of late November 2025 and the galodo disaster in Arosuka, Solok Regency, in September 2026. The study aims to identify the forms of humanitarian action, the actors involved, and the ways social solidarity is expressed through collective responses to disasters. It employs a qualitative approach with a comparative documentary study design. Data were collected from online news reports, government and disaster-management publications, organizational documentation, fundraising materials, and photographs related to humanitarian activities. The findings show that humanitarian action in the 2025 disaster involved large-scale logistical distribution across several affected areas, including the delivery of 22.7 tons of aid by air through 47 sorties between 28 November and 5 December 2025. In Arosuka, humanitarian responses included financial and material assistance, emergency personnel deployment, equipment support, and the establishment of a public kitchen. The comparison demonstrates that social solidarity is expressed through diverse forms of collective action shaped by the scale of the disaster, the needs of affected communities, and the involvement of different actors. From Durkheim’s perspective, these responses reflect social cohesion through shared concern and collective responsibility. The findings also highlight the relevance of solidarity to Islamic Community Development.

papers.title: Resilient Railways Facing Heavy Rains (RERA-Rain)
papers.summary: Abstract The Resilient Railways Facing Heavy Rains (RERA Rain) project introduces a practical framework to enhance railway resilience against increasingly frequent and intense heavy rainfall events driven by climate change. Co-developed with infrastructure managers from multiple countries, the RERA Rain Framework reflects real-world operational experience and is aligned with actual sector needs, making it both actionable and implementable. The framework addresses the urgent need to plan beyond historical climate patterns and respond to evolving hydrometeorological risks. Heavy rainfall can cause landslides, flooding, and erosion, which compromise infrastructure integrity and disrupt operations, posing serious safety and reliability challenges. Structured in three interconnected phases, the framework begins with Climate Impact Analysis, assessing projected precipitation under various climate scenarios. The second phase, Vulnerability, Risk, and Criticality Assessment, identifies high-risk assets and prioritizes them based on network relevance. Finally, the Adaptation Planning phase provides guidance for selecting and implementing risk mitigation measures. Flexible and scalable, the framework can be applied to assets, line sections, or full networks depending on data, resources, and risk exposure. It supports both strategic and technical users, enabling coordinated, proactive adaptation. The RERA Rain Framework offers a concrete tool to maintain railway safety, reliability, and sustainability under changing climate conditions.

papers.title: Nature-Based Solutions for Resilient Transport Infrastructure: Introducing the Horizon Europe NATURE-DEMO Project
papers.summary: Abstract Climate-related hazards such as flooding, wildfires, landslides and erosion increasingly stress transport infrastructure across Europe. The Horizon Europe project NATURE-DEMO addresses these challenges by linking ecological and climate science with digital engineering and practical implementation. It demonstrates how nature-based solutions (NbS) can enhance the resilience and sustainability of critical transport infrastructure. This paper introduces the project’s structure, objectives and methodological approach, with emphasis on its relevance for adaptation. A network of demonstration and replication sites, connected to different types of infrastructure, supports integration of NbS into digital planning and decision-support tools. The paper provides an overview intended to inform infrastructure managers, policymakers and researchers about scalable NbS applications in Europe.

papers.title: Incentive Structure Shapes Mitigation Behavior in a Dynamic Landslide Risk Simulator
papers.source: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
papers.summary: Decisions regarding mitigation and adaptation in terms of money in areas prone to landslides need to be made repeatedly. But, there is no evidence of how incentive structures of disaster insurance affect the mitigation process in dynamic environments of hazard. In the present study, mitigation and insurance decisions were studied using the Interactive Landslide Simulator, a microworld of Human Factors involving repeated decision-making under landslide risk. Seventy-five participants hailing from landslide-prone areas of Himachal Pradesh, India, were randomly allocated into No Insurance, Benevolent Insurance, or Smart Insurance groups and asked to perform 36 rounds of decision-making. It was found that insurance structure affected both mitigation and insurance investments. While the highest level of mitigation was observed in case of no insurance, Smart Insurance resulted in maximum insurance investment but did not enhance mitigation over Benevolent Insurance. Findings suggest that reimbursement-system design can shape risk-management behavior in disaster-risk policy.

papers.title: ResiliNet: A C++ Socket-Driven Store-and-Forward Mesh Communication Framework for Disaster-Resilient Emergency Response
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Natural disasters such as earthquakes, floods, landslides, and cyclones frequently destroy cellular base stations, sever fiber-optic backhaul links, and overload remaining communication infrastructure. When conventional mobile data and end-to-end Internet connectivity become unavailable, emergency response teams operating in disaster zones lose the ability to transmit rescue requests, GPS coordinates, damage photographs, videos, and tactical documents to central command centers. Conventional client-server messaging platforms fail completely under such partitioned or intermittent network topologies. This paper presents ResiliNet, a disruption-tolerant, disaster-resilient emergency communication platform built on store-and-forward mesh networking principles. Unlike traditional applications that require a continuous end-to-end path to a central server, ResiliNet enables participating field devices to create emergency reports, persist them locally in crash-safe storage, and opportunistically relay them across intermediate nodes whenever transient peer-to-peer links become available. The core communication engine is implemented in C++ using low-level socket programming, providing deterministic control over packet framing, non-blocking I/O, data chunking, checksum integrity verification, selective retransmission, duplicate suppression, and four-tier priority scheduling (Critical, High, Normal, and Low). When a relaying node eventually enters an area with active backhaul connectivity, an edge gateway synchronizes queued messages to a Python FastAPI backend and a React-based Central Command Dashboard, enabling coordinators to monitor live node health, queue backlogs, and verified delivery states. papers.title: Background sampling changes validation scores more than landslide susceptibility rankings
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This repository contains the reproducibility materials associated with the manuscript “Background sampling changes validation scores more than landslide susceptibility rankings”. The study examines how alternative background-sampling designs affect validation discrimination and wall-to-wall spatial ranking in machine-learning-based landslide susceptibility mapping. The analysis uses Random Forest and XGBoost models, object-aware spatial cross-validation, five background-exclusion distances (0–500 m), 20 stochastic background realizations, and 200 wall-to-wall susceptibility maps. The repository includes analysis code, model configurations, spatial fold definitions, random seeds, figure-generation materials, and non-restricted derived outputs used to reproduce the main analyses and figures reported in the manuscript. The original landslide inventory and geological/lithological source information were digitized from geoscience maps available through the Geoscience Map Viewer of the General Directorate of Mineral Research and Exploration of Türkiye (MTA). These third-party source materials are not redistributed in this repository. Publicly available environmental datasets used in the study should be obtained from their original providers. The repository is intended to support transparency, reproducibility, and independent verification of the analyses presented in the associated manuscript.

papers.title: Mapping Earth surface elevation changes using offsets between Sentinel-2, Landsat, and Sentinel-1 orthoimages from adjacent orbits
papers.summary: Abstract. Accurate digital elevation models (DEMs) are essential for orthorectifying satellite imagery, but any deviation between the orthorectification DEM and the true surface elevation at acquisition time produces horizontal offsets in the resulting orthoimages. These offsets are typically an unwanted artefact. Here, we exploit cross-track disparities between overlapping orthoimages from adjacent orbits opportunistically to retrieve elevation changes at the Earth surface. We develop the geometric framework for this orthoimage-disparity approach for both optical pushbroom sensors (Sentinel-2, Landsat 8/9) and synthetic aperture radar (Sentinel-1), and present several implementation strategies, including single differences against the orthorectification DEM, double differences between two image epochs that eliminate the reference DEM, mixed-mission combinations (e.g. Sentinel-2 with Landsat 8/9), and joint retrieval of vertical change together with horizontal surface displacement. A broad set of case studies illustrates the method across geoscientific applications: glacier thickness changes on Aletsch (Switzerland), Disappointment (Yukon), Sermeq Kujalleq (Jakobshavn isbræ, Greenland), and Southern Patagonian Ice Field; surging glaciers in Svalbard; outlet dynamics in West Antarctica; a subglacial lake drainage on Ellesmere Island; the Aru glacier detachments and the Sedongpu erosion canyon on the Tibetan Plateau; the Karrat fjord landslide (Greenland); permafrost thaw slumps in northern Canada; topographic change at Kilauea and Nishinoshima volcanoes; snow and ice change in Iceland; changes in level and volume of a reservoir (Australia), co-seismic uplift from the 2016 Kaikōura earthquake (New Zealand); and Amazon forest clear-cuts. Single orthoimage offsets reach an accuracy of roughly 1/10 of a pixel, resulting in effective elevation uncertainties of around 3–5 m. Metre-scale precision seems achievable through stacking. papers.title: A preliminary study of runoff-generated waste dump debris flow in the mountain cryosphere
papers.summary: Abstract Waste dump debris flows pose significant risks as man-made disasters. The development of large-scale infrastructure in the Tibetan Plateau of China has led to the accumulation of tunnel waste in the mountain cryosphere. To investigate the erosion process and initiation mechanism of waste dump debris flows caused by concentrated runoff in the mountain cryosphere, we examined the erosion characteristics of the Duoxiongla waste dump near Mount Namcha Barwa. Subsequently, we performed flume experiments using various waste dump geometries, considering the geomorphic and hydrological characteristics of the Longjiaqu catchment. The results reveal that the waste dump in the mountain cryosphere undergoes significant rill and lateral erosion caused by snowmelt runoff, which is further exacerbated by rainfall. Initially, the waste dump experiences headward erosion and gully erosion when subjected to simulated concentrated runoff. As the water discharge increases, the erosion gully widens and deepens, forming an erosion channel. With intensified surface runoff, the erosion channel transforms into a channelized debris flow, causing significant erosion of the channel bed. The water discharge required to trigger channelized debris flow increases with steeper slopes, assuming similar waste dump volumes. Channelized debris flow can occur when snowmelt and rainfall coincide, especially in cases of inadequate design. Hydromechanical analysis reveals that waste dump debris flow occurs as water discharge increases due to the drag force on the surface of the waste dump, seepage force inside the waste dump, and gradual saturation or near saturation of the shallow portion.

papers.title: Improved Structural Integrity of Buried Steel Pipelines Under Ground Movement Using Field Testing: Geobuffer Mitigation Technique and Distributed Fiber-Optic Monitoring

papers.summary: Buried pipelines traversing geohazard-prone regions are susceptible to failure induced by ground movements such as landslides, slope creep, and fault rupture. These deformations impose significant axial strains on pipelines, potentially leading to localized buckling or rupture. This thesis presents an integrated field-validated approach to pipeline geohazard management through two complementary strategies: the Geobuffer system as a structural mitigation technique, and Fiber Bragg Gratings-based distributed fiber-optic sensing (FBG-based DFOS) as a continuous monitoring technology. The Geobuffer is a novel engineered backfill system comprising compressible blocks installed above the pipeline to absorb ground-induced displacement and redistribute strain demands over a longer pipe length. Four full-scale field tests were conducted on NPS 8, API 5L Grade X52 steel pipeline specimens, each 23.5 m in length, subjected to 330 mm of controlled vertical uplift to simulate a landslide scarp scenario. Two tests used standard native clay backfill as a baseline and two incorporated the Geobuffer system over a 12.0 m segment. The Geobuffer system reduced peak longitudinal pipeline strain by approximately 52% based on strain gauge measurements and 67% based on finite element analysis, maintained elastic pipe behavior throughout the full uplift while the baseline pipe exceeded yield strain and sustained permanent deformation. Pipe end rotation was also reduced by 33%, from approximately 6° to 4°, reflecting a more distributed curvature response. A finite element model developed in Abaqus and validated against field measurements confirmed the experimental findings. It extended the analysis to continuous strain distributions along the full pipe length and compared the backfill vertical resistance force between the two setups. papers.title: Machine Learning-Assisted Reliability and Risk Assessment of Rock Slopes under Geotechnical Uncertainty
papers.summary: Rock-slope stability is strongly controlled by discontinuities and uncertain geotechnical parameters, while conventional deterministic factor-of-safety (FOS) calculations do not explicitly quantify the probability of failure. This study develops an integrated machine-learning (ML)-assisted framework for reliability and risk assessment of rock slopes under geotechnical uncertainty using random-field modelling and surrogate learning. Five stochastic input variables, discontinuity cohesion c^{\prime }, friction angle {\phi }^{\prime }, unit weight γ, slope height H, and face angle β, are considered, with spatial variability explicitly represented for the discontinuity-strength parameters. The deterministic planar-sliding model is calibrated to an FOS of approximately 1.20 under the mean input conditions, while 10,000 Monte Carlo simulations (MCS) yield a stochastic mean FOS of approximately 1.22 and a reference failure probability of P_{f}=0.3034. A multilayer perceptron (MLP) surrogate developed from 300 direct model evaluations is used to approximate the relationship between the stochastic inputs and FOS. The MLP achieves R^{2}=0.925, RMSE = 0.101, and MAE = 0.079, and estimates P_{f}=0.3155, corresponding to a relative difference of approximately 4.0% from the direct MCS estimate. Aleatory uncertainty is represented through the variability of the stochastic geotechnical inputs, while surrogate-related epistemic uncertainty is evaluated using bootstrap resampling. The surrogate-assisted approach reduces the number of required direct model evaluations from 10,000 to 300, substantially improving computational efficiency for reliability analysis. A consequence-based risk-screening framework further demonstrates how probabilistic reliability estimates can support monitoring and risk-mitigation decisions. The proposed framework provides a reproducible basis for extending ML-assisted rock-slope reliability analysis to site-specific numerical models and monitoring datasets.

papers.summary: CorrSurf measures surface displacement and velocity of rock glaciers, landslides, glaciers and other mass movements by area-based image matching (feature tracking) between two co-registered, orthorectified rasters: an earlier and a later image. Main features: Three matching methods: normalized cross-correlation (NCC), orientation correlation (OC) and phase correlation (PC). Sub-pixel precision by peak fitting on the correlation surface (parabolic, Gaussian, 2-D quadratic) or by bi-cubic interpolation of the image intensities before matching. Quality measures for every point (correlation peak, peak ratio, border flag) and live filters: minimum peak, minimum peak ratio, maximum displacement and the normalized median test. Back-matching check that rejects inconsistent matches. Co-registration from stable ground: shift, Helmert or affine transformation with automatic or manual outlier rejection and a residual report. Point inspector showing the reference block, the search window and the correlation surface, to tune the window sizes before a run. Velocity in m/yr from the image dates; outputs to CSV, GeoJSON points and vectors, a multi-band GeoTIFF and JSON metadata. Tiled reading of large images, matching on all CPU cores in parallel or on an NVIDIA GPU (CUDA, via CuPy). CorrSurf comes as a QGIS plugin (QGIS 3.28+ and QGIS 4) and as a standalone desktop application with a command-line tool; both share the same Python engine. It follows the image-correlation workflow described for CIAS (Kääb & Vollmer, 2000; Heid & Kääb, 2012, Debella-Gilo & Kääb, 2011) and similar image-correlation packages. It is an independent implementation written from the published methods; it does not contain or derive from CIAS code and is not affiliated with it. papers.title: CLIMATE CHANGE AND LAND-USE INTEGRATION IN GEOHAZARD ASSESSMENT: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF MODELLING APPROACHES AND IMPLICATIONS FOR ENVIRONMENTAL RISK MANAGEMENT
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Climate change and land-use change jointly influence geohazard processes and exposure, yet their interactions are not consistently represented in geohazard assessment models. This systematic review evaluates the extent of climate–land-use integration in geohazard modelling and its implications for environmental risk management. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, 2,533 studies published between 2002 and 2025 were reviewed using records from OpenAlex, Web of Science and Scopus. A five-level framework (L0–L4) was used to classify the depth of integration, from limited consideration of environmental drivers to explicit interactions and joint future scenarios. The results show substantial growth in geohazard research, particularly after 2018, dominated by landslide and flood assessments and increasing applications of GIS, remote sensing and machine learning. However, methodological diversification has not translated into comparable progress in climate–land-use integration. Only 27 studies (1.07%) met the criteria for explicit interaction or coupled-process modelling (L3) or joint future climate–land-use scenarios (L4), including five studies at L4. This finding reveals a persistent distinction between including multiple environmental predictors and modelling their combined effects. From an environmental management perspective, lower-integration approaches can support hazard characterisation and preliminary screening, whereas assessments of concurrent future climate and land-use changes require models capable of representing their interactions. Although incomplete full-text retrieval and classification uncertainty constrain the interpretation of these findings, the review provides a structured basis for assessing the suitability of modelling evidence for different management applications. papers.title: Livestock farming and soil erosion prevention ecosystem service: a RUSLE-GIS estimation in Italian alpine grassland-based dairy farms
papers.summary: The ecosystem service of erosion prevention (ESEP) becomes increasingly important due to the increasing intensity and frequency of extreme rainfall events, particularly in Italy, which records the highest soil loss rate in Europe (24.13% of total soil loss in EU; average 8.46 t ha−1 year−1). Knowledge on ESEP focuses mainly on farmland, orchards and forests, while grassland managed by mountain dairy farms have been less studied. This study uses a 2017 dataset from 38 grassland-based dairy farms in the Eastern Italian Alps. The aim was to identify the environmental and management factors that most influence soil erosion. The Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) was applied in a GIS-based framework. Monthly variation in the C factor (representing land cover and management effects) was estimated for three plots per farm (113 plots total) using a Generalised Linear Mixed Model. Although estimated mean soil loss (9.48 t ha−1 year−1) is slightly above the Italian average, nearly half of the plots have erosion rates lower than this benchmark. The C factor shows significant correlations with mean monthly temperature, altitude and species richness in the plot, fuel used per hectare and farm area. Higher temperature lowered the C-Factor, resulting in better soil protection, and the other factors increased it, though with a lower strength. This modelling study is a first step towards understanding the relative importance of factors driving mountain soil erosion. Such study could support the assessment of soil erosion in future scenarios, involving livestock farming abandonment in a context of climate change

papers.title: The 26 August 2026 Cascading Disaster at the Nepal-China Border: A Transboundary Hazard Chain and Its Implications for Early Warning
papers.source: International Journal of Disaster Risk Science
papers.summary: Abstract High Mountain Asia (HMA) as a whole is losing glacier mass at an accelerating rate since 2000, and cryosphere-related hazard chains are a growing concern. On 26 August 2026, a cascading disaster was triggered at a glacier on the slopes of Langtang Lirung (7,234 m), Nepal, and evolved within minutes into a debris flow that devastated Gyirong Port in China before re-entering Nepal as a far-traveled flood. We reconstruct the event from seismic records, rapid satellite assessments, and official reports. A peer-reviewed post-event analysis based on satellite pixel offset tracking has since documented a multi-month pre-failure acceleration of melting and ice-flow deformation of the source glacier. The avalanche that occurred at about 5,200–5,300 m a.s.l. at 10:52 Beijing time was initially cataloged as an M4.4 earthquake and later reclassified as a landslide with an equivalent seismic magnitude of 5.2. It struck Gyirong Port, roughly 20 km away, only 6–7 min after release. About 0.7 km 2 of the port area and 27 buildings were leveled, a barrier lake of up to 2.5 million m 3 formed and later drained, and the flood propagated along a river corridor more than 100 km downstream, affecting multiple districts of Nepal. Reported losses include 43 deaths and 519 missing in China (as of 5 September 2026) and 1,451 deaths and about 5,786 missing in Nepal (as of 20 September 2026). Because the source held no glacial lake and Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology reported no heavy rainfall in the source area before the event, the disaster fell outside the scope of prevailing glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) and monsoon-centric early warning arrangements. The event indicates the need for a joint China-Nepal monitoring, warning, and emergency framework for transboundary hazard chains.

papers.title: ZigBee Wireless Sensor Networks for Landslide Monitoring and Early Warning: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.summary: Landslide-monitoring systems can measure rainfall, soil conditions, and ground movement, yet transmitting sensor readings and delivering dependable warnings are distinct engineering challenges. This review examines ten published studies on ZigBee-related wireless sensor networks (WSNs) for slope monitoring, focusing on sensing architectures, communication reliability, energy management, and warning integration. Reported implementations include adaptive star/tree networking, vegetation-sensitive radio measurements, a location-specific packet-loss result, solar-supported mesh networks, and modeled sensor-node lifetime. Confirmed ZigBee systems are considered separately from mixed-frequency XBee products and related IEEE 802.15.4 implementations. Because their devices, terrain, radio configurations, and validation conditions differ, the performance results cannot be pooled into a universal reliability estimate. Some systems incorporate warning decisions, but the reviewed evidence does not establish comparable end-to-end alert latency or confirmed recipient delivery. ZigBee remains a promising technology for low-rate slope-sensor communication, provided its actual link, power, gateway, and alert performance are evaluated under site-specific conditions.

papers.title: Geographical distribution, community characteristics, and survival status of Cypripedium palangshanense, a plant species with an extremely small population
papers.summary: Cypripedium palangshanense is a plant species with an extremely small population (PSESP) and is listed among China’s first batch of priority protected species. Difficulties in population regeneration and unclear mechanisms of endangerment highlight an urgent need for systematic community ecology research to support its scientific conservation. Based on examinations of herbarium specimens and literature, combined with systematic field surveys and laboratory experiments, this study presents the first comprehensive analysis of its distribution, habitat, community structure, and reproductive capacity. The results show that: (1) Its distribution is restricted to the Minshan, Qionglai and Daba Mountain ranges, with 15 confirmed extant populations (an increase of nine compared with previous records), a vertical distribution range of 2 365–2 936 m, and a highly fragmented spatial pattern. (2) Its typical habitat is the shady, moist understory of subalpine coniferous forests with a thick moss layer. A total of 157 vascular plant species belonging to 48 families and 95 genera were recorded within its associated communities. The life-form spectrum is dominated by deciduous shrubs and perennial herbs, and the flora exhibits a North Temperate background with mixed tropical elements. (3) TWINSPAN classification divided these communities into six association groups and ten associations, indicating that C. palangshanense can occur as a companion species across various coniferous forest types. (4) It exhibits an extremely low proportion of viable seeds from sexual reproduction (ca. 14.4%) and lacks clonal reproductive capacity, resulting in weak natural population regeneration. (5) All populations are subjected to high-intensity natural disturbances (landslides, debris flows, and flooding) and anthropogenic pressures (grazing and road construction). papers.title: Simulation of the Interaction Process of a Typical Loess Landslide and River Terrace Deposit Using the Two-Phase Material Point Method
papers.summary: Landslide–terrace deposit interaction is a dominant phenomenon in some rapid loess landslides, shaping the final morphology and determining the mobility of the landslide. To investigate this interaction, we simulated the post-failure dynamic process of the Ximiaodian landslide in Shaanxi, China, using a two-phase material point model. The loess mass was modeled as a single-phase elastoplastic material, and the saturated terrace deposit via independent solid and water points. The results show that the landslide movement lasts ~20 s, producing a final terrace material uplift of ~3.5 m, consistent with measured topographic profiles. The peak mean velocity of the terrace lags the loess mass by 4.5 s, with both peak velocity and final displacement decreasing downstream. Near the slope toe, the terrace surface advances ~100 m versus 31 m at its base, demonstrating pronounced internal shear. Frontal terrace uplift decreases from ~6.0 to 3.5 m during propagation while the distal terrace remains largely undisturbed. Furthermore, pore water bears most of the total-stress increment during loading, followed by dissipation under nearly constant total stress. Under the progressive pushing and overriding of the landslide, this stress evolution of the terrace material may contribute to the final long run-out morphology of this landslide.

papers.title: GAIA: A Physics-Informed Spatio-Temporal Neural Operator with Attention Gating for Geohazard Early Warning and Landslide Risk Prediction
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: GAIA: A Physics-Informed Spatio-Temporal Neural Operator with Attention Gating for Geohazard Early Warning and Landslide Risk Prediction Abstract: Landslides represent one of the most catastrophic geohazards globally, causing severe loss of life, infrastructure degradation, and economic disruption, particularly across ecologically sensitive tropical highlands such as the Western Ghats of Kerala, India. Conventional landslide susceptibility modeling predominantly relies on either empirical limit equilibrium equations or purely data-driven statistical machine learning models, such as Random Forest and XGBoost. While data-driven models achieve high predictive correlation, they frequently lack physical interpretability and fail to generalize under extreme unseen meteorological events. In this work, we propose GAIA (Geophysical Artificial Intelligence Assistant), a novel Spatio-Temporal Physics-Informed Neural Operator with Attention Gating (ST-PINO with AG) tailored for operational geohazard early warning. GAIA employs a modular Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture comprising: Hydrological Expert: A Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) network for modeling sequential precipitation accumulation and soil moisture temporal dynamics. Geotechnical Expert: A Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) for modeling topographical terrain topology and slope proximity. Land-Use Expert: A Multi-Head Self-Attention Transformer for analyzing land cover and vegetation dynamics. Differentiable Physics Layer: An analytical Mohr-Coulomb Factor of Safety (FOS) equation embedded directly into neural attention gating to enforce mechanical slope stability laws. papers.title: Anisotropic Shrinkage and Isotropic Swelling of Kerek Formation Claystone in Semarang Regency, Central Java: A Counterintuitive Behavior Uncorrelated with Montmorillonite Content
papers.summary: Road infrastructure damage and landslides in Semarang Regency are frequently associated with the Kerek Formation claystone. This study aims to characterize the swell-shrink properties of this claystone and identify the factors controlling its volumetric behavior beyond conventional mineralogy-based approaches. Six representative samples were shaped into cubes and tested using a free swell test (unconfined method) under dry and wet conditions to measure three-axis strain (x, y, z), supported by X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) analysis. The results reveal two counterintuitive findings. First, the highest expansion occurred in a sample containing no montmorillonite, instead dominated by quartz, kaolin, and carbonates. Second, samples with very high calcite content exhibited contrasting behaviors: some showed suppressed swelling due to carbonate cementation, while others displayed moderate swelling where calcite occurred as discrete grains without forming an effective cement network. Correlation analysis shows that shrinkage is anisotropic (vertically oriented) and correlates with montmorillonite content, whereas swelling is isotropic (uniform in all directions) and shows no correlation with any single mineral.The Kerek Formation claystone exhibits decoupled directional behavior: shrinkage is anisotropic while swelling is isotropic. The occurrence of measurable swelling in montmorillonite-free samples points to alternative expansion mechanisms including microcrack closure and carbonate-related processes. These findings provide a crucial mechanical explanation for infrastructure damage in the area and demonstrate that reliable geotechnical characterization must consider whole-rock mineralogy, carbonate cementation state, and tectonic history—not merely montmorillonite content.Keywords: claystone . papers.title: Integrating Geological Research and Environmental Monitoring in Mineral Extraction: A Critical Review of Frameworks, Technologies and Research Priorities
papers.source: International Journal of Scientific Research in Science and Technology
papers.summary: Mineral extraction is expanding to supply the materials required for the energy transition, while ore grades decline and the volumes of waste per unit of metal rise.These trends increase the environmental consequences of mining and make the traditional separation between geological investigation (exploration, resource modelling) and environmental monitoring (compliance sampling, post-hoc assessment) increasingly untenable.This review synthesises the literature on how geological knowledge and environmental monitoring can be integrated across the mine life cycle.We first summarise the geological controls on environmental risk, including deposit type, mineralogy, geochemical background and the prediction of acid and metalliferous drainage.We then review the monitoring toolbox: geochemical and hydrogeochemical sampling, portable analytical methods, geophysical imaging, optical and radar remote sensing, high-frequency sensors and DNA-based biomonitoring.Integration frameworks are examined, covering geoenvironmental models, geometallurgical and geoenvironmental block models, data-driven and machine-learning approaches, and early-warning systems for tailings and slope stability, illustrated with the Brumadinho, Tisza and Amazonian gold-mining cases.We discuss governance, datastandardisation and scale-mismatch barriers, and propose a research agenda centred on shared geo-environmental data infrastructure, uncertainty-aware prediction and closure-oriented monitoring design.The review argues that environmental performance is largely determined by geology that is already known, or knowable, at the exploration stage, and that monitoring is most effective when designed from the same geological model that guides extraction.

papers.title: A Field-Oriented Workflow for Automated Detection of Microseismic Events in Creeping Landslides
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Before slope failure, rock fracturing and slip produce weak microseismic signals. Their timely detection and analysis can help identify potential failure precursors and support early warning. In the field, however, microseismic signals are often extremely weak and masked by environmental noise from wind, rainfall, flowing water, and human activities. Manual screening alone to identify these signals in large volumes of continuous data is time-consuming, and many may be missed. To address this, we developed a two-stage machine-learning method and applied it to two large creeping landslides, SeLa and Shangquesuo, in the upper Jinsha River region. First, a deep-learning model detects microseismic signals and determines their onset and termination times in single-station records. Second, an unsupervised clustering algorithm automatically associates simultaneous signals across multiple stations. During an 85-day continuous-monitoring test, the method achieved an 86.9% manual-review confirmation rate and nearly doubled the valid events compared with a conventional manual catalog, recovering many weak signals missed during manual prescreening. Comparison with InSAR-derived surface deformation showed that microseismic activity concentrated in areas of pronounced deformation and event-frequency increases generally coincided with accelerated slope deformation. This method provides a practical means of incorporating microseismic monitoring into existing landslide monitoring and early-warning systems.

papers.title: CSFS-YOLOv8n: A complex terrain landslide detection model synergistically enhanced by SCConv and SCSA
papers.summary: Landslides occur frequently in plateau and mountainous regions. Remote sensing images acquired over complex terrain typically suffer from strong background interference, weak features of small-scale landslide targets, imbalanced sample distributions, and difficulties in target localization, which make it difficult for existing detection models to balance detection accuracy with lightweight deployment requirements. To address these issues, this paper proposes CSFS-YOLOv8n, a lightweight model with high detection accuracy for remote sensing landslide detection based on the lightweight YOLOv8n network. First, the SCSA attention mechanism is introduced to enhance the network's ability to perceive weak landslide features and effectively suppress background noise interference in complex terrain. Second, a synergistic optimization of Focal Loss and SIoU loss is adopted to alleviate sample class imbalance while improving the boundary localization accuracy of landslide targets. Furthermore, the lightweight SCConv convolutional module is embedded to strengthen multi-scale feature fusion, and the AdamW optimization strategy is used to further improve convergence stability and generalization capability. Experimental results show that compared with the original YOLOv8n model, CSFS-YOLOv8n improves precision, recall, mAP@0.5, and mAP@0.5:0.95 by 2.2%, 4.5%, 3.7%, and 3.9%, respectively. Meanwhile, the parameter count increases by only 0.14% and the computational cost by only 2.47%, achieving a significant improvement in detection accuracy while maintaining real-time inference capability. The results indicate that the proposed model has strong anti-interference ability and scene adaptability in complex plateau and mountainous remote sensing scenarios, and can provide efficient and reliable technical support for intelligent landslide disaster identification, hazard investigation, and disaster prevention and mitigation.
