papers.title: When slopes awaken: Detecting landslide activation phases with InSAR and optical offset tracking
papers.summary: Abstract The Aiguilles - Pas de l’Ours landslide located near the village of Aiguilles (South-east French Alps) is one of the largest and continuously active landslides in France, with an estimated area of 18 ha. The landslide was activated in late 2016, raising concerns that the slope collapse may cause a sediment dam on the Guil River downslope. We investigate the kinematics of the Aiguilles - Pas de l’Ours landslide from 2014 to 2020 using a multi-sensor approach combining satellite-based radar interferometry (InSAR), satellite-based multi-pairwise optical image correlation (OIC), ground-based synthetic aperture radar (GB-InSAR), and ground-based Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS). We propose a strategy to invert the 3D displacement time series by combining satellite-based InSAR and OIC results. We show that merging these datasets into a 3D displacement time series significantly improves the accuracy of satellite-based displacement time series and facilitates the interpretation of complex landslide motion, in particular to detect the onset and duration of episodic accelerations. We determine the amount of rain on the ground, Rain-on-Snow (RoS), and snowmelt using in situ meteorological data, satellite-based maps of the snow cover and snow water equivalent (SWE) modelling to explain the onset of two successive episodic accelerations in winter 2016–2017 and spring 2018. Our findings highlight the importance of systematically combining several monitoring approaches to accurately capture large-scale landslides with local estimates of hydrological forcings to determine the onset of slope acceleration. These results offer perspectives for regional detection of slope episodic accelerations.

papers.title: Effects of Avalanches and the Vaia Storm on Land Use Changes and Erosion Susceptibility in the Eastern Italian Alps
papers.summary: ABSTRACT In Alpine catchments, extreme weather events and avalanches contribute to alterations in soil characteristics and land use conditions, thereby affecting hillslope stability and increasing erosion‐prone areas. The effects of major natural hazards on land use land cover (LULC) changes and erosion susceptibility remain poorly understood in steep mountainous areas. Therefore, this study aims to (i) assess the dominant LULC change dynamics using high‐resolution orthophotos before and after the 2014 and 2018 hazards (avalanches and the Vaia storm, respectively) in an Alpine catchment in northeastern Italy, (ii) develop multi‐temporal erosion susceptibility maps (ESMs) under varying LULC conditions and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) using Multi‐Criteria Decision Analysis, (iii) validate the predicted ESMs using hydrogeological hazard inventory data. Orthophoto analysis conducted for 2015 (following the 2014 avalanche events) showed localized conversion of grassland to bareland on hillslopes, particularly at high elevations. Following the Vaia storm in 2018, the catchment experienced a substantial net loss of grassland (23% reduction) and a 2% decrease in forest cover, which was largely converted into bareland. These land cover changes, together with other conditioning factors, contributed to a ~4% increase in erosion‐prone areas by 2021, with moderately susceptible hillslopes accounting for ~22% of the catchment. Slope (27.2%), LULC (13.1%), lithology (9.6%), and soil texture (7.5%) were the most influential conditioning factors in determining erosion susceptibility. Integrating temporal LULC and NDVI as dynamic factors proved effective in predicting the changes in erosion susceptibility after the considered natural hazard events.

Plant slope protection is an effective protective solution that takes into account both ecological benefits and engineering safety. papers.title: Scale-dependent landslide susceptibility assessment and model transfer: a multi-scale study in the Wenchuan–Maoxian area, China
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility models are strongly influenced by the spatial scale at which conditioning factors and landslide inventories are represented. However, whether a regional-scale factor system can be directly transferred to finer-scale assessments remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates the scale dependence of landslide susceptibility assessment in the Wenchuan–Maoxian area, southwestern China, using Random Forest models at regional and segment scales. A regional model was developed using six conditioning factors derived from 30 m DEM and Landsat imagery, while a segment-scale model incorporated 12.5 m ALOS PALSAR DEM-derived geomorphic indices and GF-2 interpreted landslide polygons. In addition, a scale-mismatch transfer experiment was conducted by applying the trained regional model to high-resolution factors over the segment area without introducing segment-specific conditioning factors. The segment model achieved the best overall performance (AUC = 0.9375; F1-score = 0.8566), whereas the transfer model showed high precision (0.9167) but lower recall (0.6667). Its recall further decreased from 0.818 for large landslides to 0.477 for small landslides, indicating limited transferability of the regional factor system to fine-scale landslide identification. Feature-importance analysis showed that the dominant conditioning factors varied with assessment scale, with river-related factors being more influential at the regional scale and tectonic and local hydrological/topographic factors becoming more important at the segment scale. These results indicate that increasing spatial resolution alone cannot compensate for the loss of process-relevant information in a scale-inappropriate factor system. Landslide susceptibility assessment should therefore match the spatial resolution, conditioning factors, and geomorphic processes to the target assessment scale.

papers.title: Bamboo Phenology as a Low-Cost, Community-Based Multidimen-sional Blind-Spot Indicator for GLOF and LDOF Cascades
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Abstract Conventional early warning systems for Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) and Landslide Dam Outburst Floods (LDOFs) in high-altitude alpine regions remain constrained by high installation costs, spatial static bias, and daytime-centric operational frameworks. Synthesising empirical disaster timelines from 2012 to 2026 across the Himalayas and the Andes, recent research demonstrates that catastrophic containment failures disproportionately breach during the pre-dawn "Dawn Cascade" (01:30–09:15 local time) and cluster across eight multidimensional blind spots—including the spatial "whack-a-mole" illusion, shoulder-season thermal traps, dry-failure mechanics, and reloaded basin sediment clocks. To bridge the monitoring gap in resource-constrained mountain corridors without relying on expensive telemetry networks, this paper proposes utilising bamboo phenology and morphological stress responses as a low-cost, community-based biological indicator system. Because native Himalayan bamboo species possess dense, shallow rhizome networks (0.3–1.0 m) that directly interact with subsurface pore-water pressure, micro-slope creep, and seasonal thermal shifts, observable changes in culm tilt, leaf curling, shoot emergence timing, and synchronous flowering provide actionable proxies for impending slope and channel instability. Integrating this botanical monitoring protocol into community-based early warning systems (CBEWS) offers an accessible, zero-power mechanism to detect hidden geohazard triggers, support United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs 11, 13, and 15), and initiate proactive nocturnal and shoulder-season evacuations.

papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Abstract While geophysical research on Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) and Landslide Dam Outburst Floods (LDOFs) has largely prioritised upstream dam-breach mechanics and hydrological routing, the downstream socio-ecological aftermath remains severely understudied. Synthesising empirical disaster timelines across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) from 2012 to 2026—including the 2021 Melamchi cascade, the 2024 Thame Valley GLOF, and the 2026 Nepalese and Bhutanese outburst floods—this study evaluates the compound impacts of nocturnal and shoulder-season cascades through an integrated One Health framework. Because catastrophic breaches disproportionately strike during the pre-dawn "Dawn Cascade" (01:30–09:15 local time) and exploit systemic monitoring blind spots, downstream communities face acute mortality alongside prolonged secondary crises in human public health, veterinary morbidity, agrarian livelihood collapse, and forced displacement. Flood-induced sewage contamination, cold-water immersion, and overcrowded relief shelters drive outbreaks of waterborne, vector-borne, and respiratory infections in humans. Concurrently, livestock—the primary economic buffer for high-altitude agro-pastoralists—suffer mass drowning, fodder starvation, water contamination, and infectious disease outbreaks, triggering distress sales and permanent livelihood abandonment. By linking low-cost biological early warning systems (such as bamboo phenology) with integrated human-veterinary post-disaster triage, this paper outlines an actionable resilience framework aligned with United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs 1, 2, 3, 11, and 13).

papers.title: Spatial phase coherence and its applications to masking and adaptive neighborhood sizing in multitemporal InSAR
papers.summary: We examine spatial phase coherence (SPC), a measure of the correlation between the wrapped phase time series of two pixels in a stack of single-look synthetic aperture radar acquisitions. A pixel and its adjacent neighbors share speckle through the point spread function, so that decorrelation alone does not lower their SPC below a floor. We find that masking pixels whose mean SPC to their eight neighbors is well below that floor, as in parts of layover and shadow areas, is an inexpensive complement to geometry-derived layover and shadow masks. For distributed scatterer pixels, averaging SPC over a fixed set of neighbors that share no speckle yields a proxy for the local coherence, the phase coherence indicator (PCI), that is available before the selection of statistically homogeneous pixels (SHPs). In phase estimation, averaging more pixels reduces noise but may also increase the bias in heterogeneous areas. To relax this trade-off, we propose to enhance SHP selection algorithms by scaling the search window size according to the PCI and truncating the set of selected pixels where a smaller nested set agrees clearly better with the phases at the center. In simulations of a TerraSAR-X and a Sentinel-1 stack with 44 and 79 acquisitions, we apply this adaptive neighborhood sizing (ANS) to established amplitude- and covariance-based SHP selection algorithms with thresholds that adapt to the PCI. Without ANS, the largest tested search window size has 13 to 29 % more phase linking error than the best of the tested sizes. With ANS, the largest window has the lowest error of the tested sizes, 11 % lower than that of the same selection at its best tested size without ANS. On a real TerraSAR-X stack, the mask based on SPC flags pixels in building shadows that a terrain model misses. On real Sentinel-1 stacks, ANS preserves dense fringes on a slowly deforming slope and in part on a fast landslide.

Methodology: This study employed quantitative spatial analysis using Landsat 8 imagery acquired in 2014 with a spatial resolution of 30 m. Land-cover classification was performed using the supervised Maximum Likelihood method in ENVI 5.1. Spatial processing, parameter scoring, and overlay analysis were conducted using ArcGIS 10.1. Field verification utilized a Garmin 76CSx GPS receiver and photographic documentation. Main Findings: The analysis identified five landslide susceptibility classes. Moderate susceptibility was dominant, covering 293,501.038 ha (74.35%), followed by high susceptibility at 53,978.392 ha (13.67%), low susceptibility at 38,851.323 ha (9.84%), and non-susceptible areas at 8,229.700 ha (2.08%). Very high susceptibility covered 198.596 ha (0.05%). Land-cover classification achieved 96.0726% overall accuracy. papers.title: Climate-driven spatio-temporal escalation of wet mass-movement disasters and their socio-economic impacts (1970−2024)
papers.summary: Abstract Mass-movement disasters, including landslides, avalanches, and mudslides, are among the most critical types of geohazards influenced by climate variability and socio-economic exposure. Climate-related and mass-movement disasters and their associated socio-economic impact data were extracted from the Emergency Events Database (EM-DAT) and aggregated at the country level to investigate global spatial patterns of disaster occurrence and impacts. The atmospheric CO 2 concentration and global mean temperature were incorporated to evaluate the climate-hazard linkages. A combination of linear regression, innovative trend analysis (ITA), and the Mann–Kendall test with Sen’s slope estimator was used to evaluate the trend characteristics and statistical significance. The findings revealed that atmospheric CO 2 concentration, global mean temperature, climate-related disasters, and mass-movement disasters increased significantly over the study period. papers.source: Journal of Geophysical Research Machine Learning and Computation
papers.summary: Abstract As a highly destructive geological hazard, landslides require accurate monitoring, and prediction for effective disaster mitigation. However, many current deep learning‐based methods for predicting landslide displacement still struggle to achieve high accuracy and to explain landslide behaviors. To address this long‐standing problem, we proposed a generative deep learning model with high accuracy and explainability for continuously predicting landslide displacement. Herein, we used 10‐day resolution and both displacement and pore pressure data. To enhance explainability, our model integrates the pore (water) pressure, which can modulate landslide displacement, by estimating the landslide acceleration probability. Furthermore, the structure of the generative model facilitates the identification of long‐term patterns and enables a more accurate prediction of landslide displacement. Experiments on two typical slow‐moving landslides in Oregon monitored with extensometers and piezometers show that compared with the best‐performing baseline models, MG‐DS reduces Root Mean Square Error and Mean Absolute Error by 11.8% and 16.1% for the Johnson Creek landslide and by 21.2% and 31.5% for the Carmel Knoll landslide, respectively. The model advantages manifest in three aspects: first, the generative model uses parallel prediction and iterative refinement to effectively enhance the accuracy; second, the model is able to identify and leverage pore pressure–displacement variations; and third, the use of a temporal decomposition architecture balances explainability and accuracy. Our study not only demonstrates that explicitly integrating pore pressure improves prediction performance but also shows that generative models provide a promising approach for landslide displacement prediction.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are a major geological hazard in hilly regions, often resulting in loss of life, damage to infrastructure, and environmental degradation. An integrated methodology for landslide susceptibility assessment is presented in this study, utilizing geospatial technology and ground-based observations. Twelve landslide-conditioning factors were integrated using an Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP)-based weighted overlay analysis within a GIS framework. Multiple thematic layers such as IRS LISS-III satellite imagery, drainage networks, slope, aspect, geology, geomorphology, and land use were processed and analyzed within a GIS framework to generate landslide susceptibility zones through a weighted index overlay technique. Using a multi-criteria evaluation approach, the study identifies and classifies landslide-prone areas, with rainfall particularly the extreme event of December 1, 2024 (238 mm) emerging as a key triggering factor. The high landslide susceptibility observed across large parts of the Shevaroyan Hills is mainly controlled by dense drainage networks, extensive road cut excavations, and unfavorable hard rock geological conditions, particularly highly weathered and fractured charnockite and gneiss formations interspersed with clay-rich zones. papers.title: Coupled seismic-seepage modelling of a bridge abutment slope and its stabilisation using geotextile gabion mattresses
papers.summary: The sequential occurrence of earthquakes and rainfall presents a profound and often underestimated threat to slope stability, particularly in tropical regions. This study addresses this critical gap through a sophisticated coupled numerical analysis of a bridge abutment slope in Sarawak, Malaysia, evaluating a novel stabilisation strategy against this combined threat. Using an advanced sequential modelling framework in GeoStudio, this study integrates dynamic seismic analysis, QUAKE/W with subsequent transient seepage simulation, SEEP/W to replicate the multi-hazard condition. Results from this study demonstrate that the synergistic effect of seismic shaking and post-earthquake rainfall infiltration drives the slope to a critical state reducing the factor of safety to 0.94 due to mechanisms of tensile cracking and pore-pressure amplification. This study shows that the application of a geotextile-reinforced gabion mattress effectively restores slope stability, increasing the factor of safety to a stable value 2.2. This study provides a critical validation of a cost-effective reinforcement technique and establishes an essential coupled modelling framework, offering a robust scientific basis for enhancing the resilience of infrastructure in seismically active and rainfall-prone regions globally.

papers.title: Landslide susceptibility assessment in the monsoon-dominated Sikkim Himalayan region using state-of-the-art models

The major findings of this research highlight that DLNN is the most effective tool for assessing LSM, proving to be more accurate than alternative methods. The LSM depicts that the southern part of the study area poses high landslide susceptibility than the other parts. The AUC‒ROC curve successfully validated the model, which is 89.90 % for DLNN, 87.20% for RF and 81.10% for DT. More participation of local communities, along with strict governmental policies, could be effective in mitigating landslides in the SHR. Adaptation of advanced RS and GIS, along with hybrid models (deep learning and soft computing), could be important tools to assess LSM more accurately.

This study investigates the northwestern slope of an open-pit coal mine near an existing lake, using field-constrained seepage analysis, finite-element limit analysis (FELA), and interpretable machine learning. A two-dimensional OptumG2 model is validated against the monitored groundwater pattern, and upper- and lower-bound FELA solutions are used to evaluate the effects of lake-water depth, lake-pit distance, waste-dump surcharge, and dump-pit setback. Increasing lake-water depth from 0 to 30 m reduced the lower- and upper-bound safety factors from 1.405 and 1.433 to 1.125 and 1.142, respectively, with the seepage-establishment stage (0–1 m) accounting for about 64% of the total stability loss and the 0–5 m interval accounting for about 68%. At a water depth of 30 m, shortening the lake-pit distance from 1200 to 600 m reduced the mean safety factor from approximately 1.13 to 1.00, with stronger sensitivity below about 800 m. Waste-dump loading exerted a secondary but significant effect: increasing surcharge from 500 to 2000 kPa at a 50 m setback reduced the lower-bound safety factor by about 6.1%, whereas increasing the setback to 200–300 m markedly weakened load–slope interaction. An XGBoost surrogate, validated via a strict blocked approach, achieved a realistic test R2 of 0.845, and SHAP analysis (with corrected physical units) identified lake-water depth and lake-pit distance as the dominant controls. The most unfavorable condition combines high lake level, short lake-pit distance, high surcharge, and short dump setback, providing a quantitative basis for monitoring, mine-layout optimization, and slope-risk management.

These units are used to analyze the SOC spatial distribution patterns along the warming gradients in different regions of China and their related variability. Through linear regression, machine learning and neighborhood least squares fitting, the main driving factors of SOC space changes on multiple scales have been determined. The results show that SOC has a strong correlation with temperature and presents a nonlinear pattern in a higher temperature range. In most areas, the initial SOC content is the dominant factor related to SOC changes, and its constraint effect increases with the increase of soil depth. In contrast, vegetation coverage and precipitation show a stronger correlation on the surface, and there is obvious regional heterogeneity. In areas with low initial carbon content, high vegetation coverage and good moisture conditions, the estimated SOC increase is often greater. With the increase of temperature and soil depth, the content of organic carbon in the soil gradually decreases, and the area of high-content areas gradually shrinks. By establishing a spatial analysis framework that combines ecological units and environmental gradients, this study enhances the regional understanding of SOC change patterns and provides a scientific basis for assessing the distribution of soil carbon in China and formulating regional management strategies. These results should be interpreted as a general response patterns, rather than an accurate prediction of the future SOC dynamics.

papers.title: Mechanisms of Channel Bank Erosion During Ice-Covered Periods
papers.summary: Riverbank erosion constitutes a prevalent phenomenon in fluvial alluvial systems and often leads to hydrogeological hazards such as bank failure and soil loss. In contrast to open-channel flow conditions, the mechanisms of bank erosion during ice-covered periods are more complex. Therefore, investigating riverbank slope stability under ice-covered conditions is essential for bank protection, riverbed evolution analysis, and river regulation in ice-affected rivers. In the present study, based on soil mechanics theory, an analytical mechanical equilibrium framework is established to formulate the stability equation for cohesive riverbanks under ice-covered conditions. Key parameters are investigated, including the critical bank height ratio, riverbed scouring depth, and lateral erosion distance under varying ice-cover thicknesses and stress conditions during the initial and stable freeze-up periods. The established equation is verified using river width data derived from satellite imagery and is applied to the Inner-Mongolia reach of the Yellow River, showing good agreement with monitored field results. The calculated results indicate that, compared with open-channel flow scenarios, ice cover alters the near-bank flow field to increase the hydrodynamic scour potential at the bank toe, while raising the critical failure threshold of riverbanks and permitting a greater scour magnitude before bank failure. Furthermore, the downstream segments of the Inner-Mongolia Reach exhibit a higher pre-failure scour threshold under ice-covered conditions than upstream areas. Taking the Toudaoguai cross-section as an example, under a 0.6-m-thick ice cover and a 50 kPa ice stress, compared with open-channel flow, the initial critical bank height ratio increases by 0.2350 (22.1%), the allowable riverbed scouring depth before failure increases by 0.7050 m (364.2%), and the allowable lateral deformation increment increases by 0.4826 m (332.6%).

Experimental Study on Crumb Rubber Modified Porous Asphalt Pavement for Enhancing Groundwater Recharge
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Prajakta Amar Pattanshetti, J. A. Patil
papers.summary: The increasing development of impervious urban surfaces has contributed to higher stormwater runoff and reduced natural groundwater recharge. Porous asphalt pavement provides an effective alternative by allowing rainfall to infiltrate through interconnected air voids. The present study experimentally investigates the use of crumb rubber in porous asphalt pavement to improve its engineering performance while promoting waste tyre utilization. Crumb rubber is incorporated at different contents, and the effect of modification is evaluated through basic bitumen properties including penetration, softening point, and ductility. Porous asphalt mixtures are further assessed for Indirect Tensile Strength (ITS) and permeability to determine the combined mechanical and hydraulic performance. The experimental results are compared to identify the crumb rubber content providing a suitable balance between pavement strength and water infiltration capacity. The study also considers the potential of porous asphalt for enhancing groundwater recharge and reducing surface runoff. A cost–benefit analysis is included to evaluate the economic feasibility of incorporating waste crumb rubber in porous asphalt pavement. The study aims to establish a practical and sustainable pavement solution that combines improved performance, groundwater recharge, waste tyre utilization, and economic benefits.

papers.title: XDA28010202 Principles and Key Technologies for Erosion Resistance Enhancement and Runoff Regulation of Black Soil on Sloping Farmland: Dataset on Runoff Regulation and Erosion Control via Erosion-Resistant and Water-Retaining Materials
papers.summary: This dataset consists of long-term positioned monitoring data obtained from field monitoring plots of erosion-resistant and water-retaining material technology in the Hailun demonstration area from 2022 to 2025. It is primarily used to evaluate the regulatory effects of erosion-resistant and water-retaining material technology on soil structure, soil water infiltration, rainfall runoff, sediment loss, and crop production in sloping cropland. The dataset covers soil background physicochemical properties, soil pore characteristics, soil aggregate composition, rainfall runoff and sediment loss, as well as crop yield and biomass in the erosion-resistant and water-retaining material monitoring plots.

papers.title: LITERATURE REVIEW ON MODIFIED DOTCON-BASED PERMEABLE PAVEMENT SYSTEM FOR URBAN FLOOD MITIGATION AND RAINWATER HARVESTING
papers.summary: Rapid urbanisation and the increase in impervious surfaces have affected the natural movement of rainwater, contributing to surface runoff, water accumulation and urban flooding.Permeable pavement systems have been studied as an alternative to conventional impermeable pavement because they allow rainwater to pass through the pavement structure and enter the underlying layers.Pervious concrete and permeable pavement systems also provide opportunities for stormwater management, groundwater recharge and rainwater harvesting.The literature reviewed in this paper covers the hydrological performance of permeable pavements, mechanical properties of pervious concrete, pavement design under traffic loading, rainwater harvesting systems and water-quality performance.The reviewed studies indicate that pavement performance depends on the properties of the surface layer, aggregate base and sub-base, underlying soil, and the provision of suitable drainage and storage arrangements.The literature also identifies the importance of balancing permeability and structural strength and considering clogging and maintenance during pavement design.The present project proposes a modification of the DOTCON-based permeable pavement concept by incorporating an additional rainwater collection, filtration and storage arrangement.The proposed modification aims to collect a portion of the water passing through the pavement and make it available for potential non-potable reuse while retaining the stormwatermanagement function of the pavement.This review provides the technical background and identifies the research requirements for evaluating the proposed system.

papers.title: How does intercropping perennial grains with alfalfa impact soil physical and hydraulic properties?
papers.summary: Perennial cereal–legume intercropping systems are promoted as climate-smart and resilient alternatives to annual monocultures; however, their effects on soil physical and hydraulic properties remain poorly quantified, particularly for developed perennial cereals; ACE1 perennial rye ( Secale cereale L.) and intermediate wheatgrass (IWG) ( Thinopyrum intermedium ). This study evaluated how intercropping these perennial cereal grain crops (PCGCs) with alfalfa ( Medicago sativa L. ) influences soil physical structure and hydraulic functioning across five field locations in Alberta, Canada. Sites were established in spring 2022, and soils were sampled in summer 2024. Using a split–split plot design, we assessed crop utilization (forage or grain), seeding arrangement, and crop treatment (intercrop or monocrop) effects on soil physical and hydraulic properties at 10–15 and 30–35 cm depths. Topsoil organic carbon (SOC) stock was also measured at 0–15 cm depth increment. Intercropping enhanced soil hydraulic properties in a site-specific manner. Compared to monocultures, PCGC–alfalfa intercrops increased field capacity (FC), plant-available water capacity (PAWC), and meso and microporosity by 6–45 %, with stronger effects at 30–35 cm depth. Unsaturated hydraulic conductivity varied among sites, but IWG-based intercrops exhibited 20–40 % higher values than ACE1 under comparable management. SOC–hydraulic relationships were context dependent; intercrops strengthened SOC water retention linkages, particularly at high-carbon sites. Multivariate analyses associated intercrops with improved water retention, pore connectivity, and S-index, whereas monocrops aligned with increased bulk density and reduced hydraulic function. Overall, intercropping PCGCs with alfalfa improved soil hydraulic functioning, primarily through enhanced water dynamics rather than major structural change, highlighting their potential to increase soil resilience across diverse environments.

papers.title: XDA28010202 Principles and Key Technologies for Erosion Resistance Enhancement and Runoff Regulation of Black Soil on Sloping Farmland: Dataset on Runoff Regulation and Erosion Control via Rapid Infiltration Zone Technology
papers.summary: This dataset consists of long-term positioned monitoring data obtained from field monitoring plots of rapid infiltration zone technology in the Hailun demonstration area from 2022 to 2025. It is primarily used to evaluate the regulatory effects of rapid infiltration zone technology on soil structure, soil water infiltration, rainfall runoff, sediment loss, and crop production in sloping cropland.The dataset covers soil background physicochemical properties, soil pore characteristics, soil aggregate composition, soil saturated hydraulic conductivity, in situ infiltration characteristics, rainfall runoff and sediment loss, as well as crop yield and biomass in the rapid infiltration zone monitoring plots.

papers.title: Maintenance Priorities for Permeable Structures and Conventional Stormwater Drainage in Ilala, Tanzania
papers.summary: Stormwater maintenance must address both the infiltration function of permeable structures and the conveyance function of conventional drainage. This study identifies maintenance concerns in Ilala, Dar es Salaam, and develops a condition-based framework for managing the two asset groups together. A descriptive reanalysis used tabulated aggregate questionnaire counts from 52 drainage personnel and service providers, along with 10 archival records of rainfall and outlet volumes. Fifty-five questionnaires were distributed, 53 were returned, and 52 were retained. Six technical domains were examined. Means and sample standard deviations were recalculated from the response counts, and indicator direction was checked against the questionnaire anchors before constructing relative severity indices. Inlet or matrix clogging had the highest severity index in both asset groups, at 0.846. Conduit blockage or loss of subsurface storage followed, at 0.819 for conventional drainage and 0.815 for permeable structures. Treatment effectiveness received favourable ratings, whereas retention and attenuation ratings indicated a need for further performance investigation. Vegetation required separate interpretation because channel obstruction and the vitality of designed planting were scored in opposite directions. Across the archival records, the aggregate fraction of rainfall volume absent from the recorded outlet was 60.1% for permeable structures and 23.1% for conventional drainage. These figures describe incomplete water balances and do not establish treatment effects or validate a predictive model. The proposed framework links inspection, sediment control, maintenance, and verification while retaining structural safety and storm-capacity checks. The findings support coordinated maintenance of infiltration and conveyance, with field measurements needed to establish hydraulic benefits, determine appropriate intervention thresholds, and assess performance changes after maintenance.

papers.title: Synergistic effects of multiple factors on surface runoff initiation time at mountainous hillslopes: A case study in the upper reach of the Danjiangkou Reservoir, China
papers.summary: Study region The Guanshan River watershed, China. Study focus Predicting surface runoff initiation time ( T sur ) is critical for flash flood early warning in mountainous watersheds. We quantified how rainfall intensity ( RI ), slope gradient ( S ), soil thickness distribution pattern ( STDP ), and initial soil moisture ( θ ini ) jointly regulate T sur through 72 laboratory simulations and 26 field plots. Three-way ANOVA decomposed the main and interaction effects, and two threshold models derived from the fitted T sur model ( CR and CR + ASM ) were validated on independent field plots. New hydrological insights for the region T sur decreased with RI and θ ini , each following a power function. The accelerating effect of S depended on RI : raising S from 5° to 15° and 25° shortened T sur by 60.5% and 75.1% at 30 mm/h but only 33.0%–66.0% at 120 mm/h, reflecting a shift from lateral-drainage to infiltration excess. RI × S and the STDP -involving interactions explained 19.19%–20.07% and 30.96%–34.87% of T sur variance, showing STDP acts as a pathway regulator, not a direct control. The fitted T sur model yielded cumulative rainfall ( CR ) thresholds CR 1 – CR 4 that partition runoff generation into three stages; which differed between thick and thin soil layers ( CR 4 = 38.64 vs. 32.67 mm) because CR alone ignores the initial storage deficit. Reformulating this criterion as CR + ASM ≥ W crit nearly eliminated this difference (≤2.32 mm) and reproduced runoff initiation under extremely dry conditions where rainfall-only indicators failed.

papers.title: Rainfall-Runoff Simulation and Hydrological Response Assessment using SWAT Model in an Urban Watershed
papers.summary: Rapid urbanization and climate variability have substantially altered the hydrological response of urban watersheds, resulting in increased surface runoff, reduced infiltration, and a higher frequency of urban flooding. Understanding these changes is essential for sustainable watershed management and flood risk mitigation. This study evaluates the rainfall-runoff response of the Wakad urban watershed in the Mula River Basin, Pune, India, using the soil and water assessment tool (SWAT) implemented through the QSWAT interface. A high-resolution modelling framework was developed using a 30 m digital elevation model (DEM), 10 m land use/land cover (LULC) data, FAO soil data, and daily hydro-meteorological data obtained from NASA POWER for the period 1995-2023. The watershed was delineated into 28 sub-basins and corresponding hydrological response units (HRUs) to represent the spatial variability of terrain, land use, and soil characteristics. Model calibration and validation were performed using SWAT-CUP with the SUFI-2 algorithm. The calibrated model showed satisfactory performance, with a Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) of 0.72 and a coefficient of determination (R²) of 0.78, indicating reliable simulation of streamflow. The simulation results revealed that increasing urbanization and expansion of impervious surfaces significantly increased surface runoff and reduced infiltration within the watershed. Peak runoff occurred during high-intensity monsoon events, with substantial temporal and spatial variability among sub-basins. The spatial distribution of runoff identified highly urbanized areas as being more susceptible to elevated runoff generation compared with relatively vegetated areas. The findings demonstrate the capability of the SWAT model to quantify long-term hydrological responses to land-use change in a rapidly urbanizing watershed. The study provides valuable hydrological information that can support watershed planning, flood risk assessment, and sustainab

papers.title: IMPACTS OF CONTEMPORARY GLOBAL CHANGES ON THE WATER CYCLE OF THE BRESTNITSA KARST GEOSYSTEM IN NORTHERN BULGARIA
papers.summary: Brestnitsa Karst Geosystem (BKG) was formed in the Pre-Balkans in Northern Bulgaria.It is developed in Mesozoic organogenic limestones with a very high carbonate content.A complete karst morphological complex has been formed in the relief of the geosystem, which is the result of the combination of autogenous and allogenic types of karst.The BKG region is located in the transitional area between the subtropical and temperate climate.The karst aquifer is recharged by infiltration through the aeration zone of precipitation, irrigation and waste household and fecal waters from livestock farms and inflow of river waters and periodic surface runoff of precipitation waters into sinkholes.The specific structure of the karst geosystem is the reason why its water cycle is very sensitive to global changes of both natural and anthropogenic types and is highly vulnerable to pollution (mechanical, chemical, bacteriological).This is a serious problem, because the geosystem drains into the karst spring Glava Panega, which is the highest flow concentrated spring in Bulgaria.Its waters are used for industrial and drinking-domestic water supply.The aim of this study is to track and analyze the consequences of global changes on the water cycle through application of a geosystem approach and the original model for integrated monitoring of karst geosystems (MIKS).Special attention is paid to the sources of anthropogenic pressure influenced by socio-economic changes in regional, national and global aspects and their impact on the pollution of karst waters.

papers.title: A practical poroelasticity modeling framework for saturated and unsaturated soils: theory, implementation, and experimental validation
papers.summary: Abstract Over the past decades, numerous poroelasticity theories have been developed to describe soil behavior from saturated to unsaturated conditions. However, existing approaches often rely on extensive auxiliary variables, complex state tracking, and intricate constitutive formulations. In many cases, reliance on full Newton–Raphson linearization and multivariable state tracking leads to high computational costs, stability issues, and diminished transparency. This paper presents a practical poroelasticity framework that provides a seamless transition between saturated and unsaturated soil behavior. The framework adopts Biot’s reciprocal coupling structure through a common αχ coupling coefficient and requires only two primary unknowns (displacement and matric potential). The formulation is implemented in FEniCS as an open-source solver, with the Bishop parameter χ updated at each time step via the Khalili–Khabbaz formula to maintain coupling accuracy throughout the saturation range. Because the nonlinear coefficients are evaluated at the previous time step, each time step requires only a single linear solve. Systematic validation against more than ten laboratory experiments and a large-scale test across diverse seepage conditions and soil types yielded strong agreement in predicting settlement, pore pressure, and water content evolution. The open-source implementation provides a reproducible and extensible computational tool for practical geotechnical applications.

papers.title: Fresh and degraded maize shoot and root residues temporarily change hydraulic properties of a loamy soil
papers.summary: Mulching and incorporation of crop residues (CR) into soils are common strategies to sustain soil carbon stocks, return nutrients, and regulate water losses through bare soil evaporation. To date, implementing the effects of mulching strategies into soil-plant-atmosphere models remains a challenge as there is limited information on how this layer of CR changes with time and how it thereby influences processes such as evaporation, water infiltration or the transport of pollutants. An important, hitherto unknown key property of a mulch layer and the incorporation of plant residues is their influence on soil hydraulic properties (SHP) as well as on the persistence of these effects over time. We hypothesized that increasing amounts of incorporated maize CR increases water retention and reduces unsaturated hydraulic conductivity, and that the quality of the CR would determine the persistence of the effects, i.e., that mulching with relatively fast decaying shoot residues would be less persistent than incorporating root residues. In a laboratory study, we quantified the effect of maize CR in various concentrations (0 wt %, 2 wt %, and 5 wt %) on the SHP of a loam soil and additionally measured the SHP of a mulch layer (100 wt % CR) from saturation to oven dryness. We differentiated between shoot and root CR to quantify the effect of biomass quality and adapted the simplified evaporation method to measure the hydraulic properties of 100 % CR layer. The experiments were run in triplicate in a climate constant room (20 °C, 65 % RH) and repeated after three weeks of incubation under optimal conditions for biological activity (30 °C, 90 % RH) to simulate organic matter degradation after harvest. CR decay was monitored by carbon and nitrogen composition of fresh material, after the first measurement of SHP (pre-incubation) and at the end of the experiment (post-incubation, incubation plus second measurement of SHP). Comparing the SHP with different CR mixtures provided direct i

papers.title: Land Use and Land Cover Change and Its Implications for Soil Erosion in the Gebre Korke Watershed, Central Ethiopia, 1995–2020
papers.summary: Abstract Land use and land cover (LULC) change is a major driver of soil degradation and declining agricultural productivity in the Ethiopian highlands. This study analyzes LULC dynamics and their implications for soil erosion in the Gebre Korke watershed (4,653.46 ha), Central Ethiopia, using multi-temporal Landsat imagery (1995, 2005, 2015, 2020), GIS techniques, and the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE). Supervised maximum-likelihood classification was applied to TM and OLI imagery with training data collected during field campaigns and verified using Google Earth high-resolution imagery. The results reveal significant LULC transformation over the 25-year study period: cultivated land expanded by 38.6%, from 1,676.0 ha (36.0%) in 1995 to 2,322.7 ha (49.9%) in 2020, while grassland and shrubland declined by 38.4% (2,027.0 ha to 1,249.5 ha) and 63.2% (1,275.5 ha to 469.5 ha), respectively. Forest cover remained relatively stable at 6–7% but decreased in absolute terms from 327.0 ha to 278.0 ha. The LULC change significantly impacted soil erosion: RUSLE analysis showed a 40.2% increase in mean annual soil loss from 18.5 t/ha/yr in 1995 to 25.9 t/ha/yr in 2020, with total soil loss rising from 86,088.0 to 120,524.5 ton/yr. The area classified as high to very high erosion risk increased from 8.0% (372.3 ha) to 18.5% (860.9 ha). The cover-management factor (C-factor) increased by 28.4% over the period, directly reflecting the erosion of protective grassland and shrubland vegetation and the expansion of erodible cropland. The study demonstrates that LULC change is the dominant anthropogenic driver of increased soil loss in the Gebre Korke watershed and underscores the urgent need for land use planning, sustainable intensification, and community-based watershed management to reverse degradation trends and safeguard the region's agricultural and ecological future.

papers.title: Long-term agricultural water conservation under straw and plastic mulching characterized with stable water isotope tracing
papers.summary: Soil health and water resource efficiency are key aspects of sustainable agriculture, and various mulching practices can contribute towards improved soil water conservation and crop yields. A 13-year long-term experiment was conducted to comparatively analyze the long-term effects of straw mulching and plastic mulching on soil properties, winter wheat physiological characteristics and yields. Stable water isotope tracing was used to analyze spatio-temporal distributions of soil water fluxes and root water uptake, so that the mechanisms whereby mulching influences soil water conservation and plant water availability can be further characterized. Results showed that both mulching practices increased the proportion of macroaggregates (>0.25 mm) (31.7%-41.6%), water content at field capacity (3.5%-7.9%), saturated hydraulic conductivity (54.9%-89.1%), leaf photosynthesis, instantaneous water use efficiency (WUE 0 ) (13.7%-34.6%), and winter wheat yields (6.9%-19.2%) compared with the control. Straw mulching was more effective than plastic mulching in reducing soil bulk density, promoting organic carbon and total nitrogen accumulation. Plastic mulching led to similar long-term cumulative yields, more consistent annual yields, and less long-term soil quality improvement than straw mulching. Stable water isotope tracing indicated that winter wheat mainly used water from the shallowest 40 cm of soil, and that both mulches improved plant water availability likely by reducing subsurface drainage losses. Additionally, plastic mulching inhibited early topsoil evaporation during the critical jointing stage. Therefore, straw mulching facilitates long-term soil improvement, whereas plastic mulching stabilizes yields under acute droughts. Further research comparing mulch types across different agricultural systems and geographical regions may enhance the generalizability of these single-site findings.

papers.title: Soil moisture dynamics and rainfall responses during citrus orchard development on sloping red soils: Evidence from five years of monitoring
papers.summary: Citrus orchards are widely distributed and ecologically important artificial ecosystems in subtropical regions worldwide, where soil water dynamics govern fruit yield and regional hydrological cycling. However, our understanding remains limited regarding how soil moisture dynamics in citrus orchards change over successive years after transplanting. Using five years (2021–2025) of high-frequency soil moisture data, we investigated changes in layered soil water storage, rainfall response characteristics, and their potential contributing factors in citrus orchards. Results showed that the soil water surplus of citrus orchards over bare land diminished progressively over years after transplantation, and the water consumption center shifted downward. Piecewise linear regression identified early 2024 (the beginning of the fourth year after transplantation) as a breakpoint. After that, the relative difference in soil water content between the citrus orchard and bare land decreased more rapidly in the middle and deep soil layers, with slope changes of −0.841 and −1.295% yr −1 , respectively. Concurrently, the attenuation of rainfall recharge in the shallow and middle layers intensified and then recovered somewhat. In contrast, deep soil water increment was mainly controlled by heavy rainfall and underwent severe attenuation, with a stronger negative correlation with antecedent moisture content. These findings reveal a breakpoint at which long-term citrus cultivation triggers a rapid decline in soil moisture, leading to deep-layer deficits. This supports adaptive irrigation based on deep-layer deficit early warning and provides a theoretical foundation for sustainable orchard management.

papers.title: Investigating the Spread and Hydrogeological Controls of Coliform Bacteria within the Kakamega Groundwater System, Western Kenya
papers.source: East African Journal of Environment and Natural Resources
papers.summary: In rural and urban Kenya, reliance on groundwater resources has expanded rapidly to meet the rising domestic and agricultural demands. However, microbial contamination presents a constant public health risk, particularly via the spread of pathogen indicators such as Escherichia coli (E. coli). This study investigated the spatial-temporal distribution and groundwater controls governing microbial spread across the three zones (Lurambi, Mumias East and Malava) in Kakamega region. Water samples were collected across 141 stations that comprised 83 deep boreholes (> 45m bgl), 26 shallow wells and 32 protected springs during biannual sampling in the dry and wet seasons. Stratified Random Sampling was applied in identifying the stations for sampling. Microbial analysis was conducted using membrane filtration on M-ColiBlue24 broth media, paired with field measurements of physio-chemical parameters (pH, EC, TDS, turbidity and temperature), water levels, and geospatial data on possible contamination sources nearby. Geospatial mapping, interpolation, the Groundwater Quality Index (GWQI) and piezometric maps were integrated to delineate vulnerability zones and possible groundwater flow direction. Microbial densities were highest in springs, heavily driven by agricultural runoff and open sanitation. Shallow wells exhibited low dry-season records and high wet-season E. coli spikes caused by rapid vertical recharge through the vadose zone and macropore flushing. Deep boreholes demonstrated lower overall contamination due to thick unsaturated zone filtration, though positive detection occurred in boreholes with shallow water tables and those in close proximity to spring discharge zones or close to hydraulic connectivity to contaminated shallow aquifers. Most of the boreholes that have been drilled by the Water Project (TWP) organisation in Kakamega region have recorded shallow water strike levels ranging from 10m bgl to 50m bgl at the contact zones of the regolith layer and stable r

papers.title: Life-cycle reliability of an unsaturated slope under stochastic rainfall–earthquake sequences: A state-continuous MPM–PDEM framework
Soil quality index as a predictor of wetting-front dynamics under surface drip irrigation
papers.summary: Efficient soil water movement is essential for improving crop water-use efficiency under drip irrigation, yet the role of Soil Quality Index (SQI) in predicting wetting-front under surface drip irrigation has not been comprehensively studied. This study investigated five land-use systems—bare fallowing for 2 years (BF2), bare fallowing for 3 years (BF3), monocropping (MOC), crop rotation (CR), and fallowing with vegetation (FV)—on soil quality and wetting-front development under surface drip irrigation. Soil hydro-physical and chemical properties at 0–30 cm depth were assessed, including bulk density (BD), water-holding capacity (WHC), pH, effective cation exchange capacity (ECEC), available phosphorus (P) and potassium (K), organic carbon (OC), total nitrogen (N), and base saturation (Bsat). Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to derive the Soil Quality Index (SQI), while wetting width and depth were measured after 15, 30, and 60 min of irrigation. Land-use management significantly (P 0.70 and reaching 0.984 between SQI and wetting depth at 60 min. The principal component regression model explained 92.75% of SQI variability. These findings demonstrate that vegetation-based fallowing and crop rotation enhance soil quality and water movement, supporting sustainable irrigation water management.

papers.title: Contour Based Ecological Landscape Restoration in the Torhasan Pond Micro Watershed
papers.summary: Global climate change and land-use alterations induce hydro-ecological challenges such as increased surface runoff and soil erosion at the watershed scale. This study proposes a contour-based ecological restoration model centered on nature-based solutions for the Torhasan Pond micro-watershed in Çanakkale, Türkiye. Micro-topographic adjustments, vegetative buffer strips, and bioswales were integrated within a holistic landscape framework. Hydrological analyses indicate that the proposed hybrid model reduces the existing surface runoff coefficient (C=0.45) to 0.20–0.25, significantly decreasing the annual runoff volume. Furthermore, spatial revegetation based on hydro-functional criteria aims to control erosion, improve water quality, and foster habitat continuity.

papers.title: The Tiber River Mouth Linear Park: A Landscape-Based Strategy for Flood Adaptation Through Nature-Based Solutions
papers.summary: Flood vulnerability at the mouth of the Tiber River is increasingly influenced by the interaction of extreme rainfall, fragmented urbanization, surface impermeability, and ecological degradation. This study develops a landscape-based flood adaptation strategy for the lower Tiber River corridor by integrating hydrological analysis with a research-by-design framework and Nature-Based Solutions (NBS). Territorial assessment, field observations, GIS-based watershed analysis, Digital Elevation Model (DEM) processing, rainfall-event analysis, and exploratory hydrological modelling using the Storm Water Management Model (SWMM) were combined to evaluate runoff dynamics, infiltration patterns, and spatial vulnerability. The analyses identified clear relationships between land cover, watershed characteristics, and runoff response, distinguishing highly impermeable sectors requiring intervention from areas with greater ecological resilience and infiltration capacity. The resulting hydrological and spatial evidence was translated into a landscape strategy incorporating wetlands, vegetated retention systems, permeable public spaces, ecological corridors, and riverbank restoration within a proposed linear park. The study demonstrates that exploratory hydrological modelling can support landscape planning by translating environmental processes into spatial design decisions, extending its role beyond engineering assessment. The proposed framework offers a transferable approach for integrating climate adaptation, ecological restoration, and resilient river-corridor planning in vulnerable Mediterranean coastal landscapes.

papers.title: SCS-CN and Green-Ampt Loss Models in Rain-on-Grid Flood Modelling: Antecedent State, Run-On Infiltration and Multi-Pulse Response
papers.summary: Rain-on-grid models of small Mediterranean catchments require a loss model, usually the SCS Curve Number (SCS-CN) or the Green-Ampt (GA) methods, rarely tested inside two-dimensional solvers. This study compares the two methods as implemented in the same TUFLOW HPC model of the Aron stream (37.5 km², southern Italy), for the multi-pulse flood of 12–13 February 2026, under radar and rain-gauge forcing. Lacking discharge data, the comparison is evaluated on a sensitivity analysis of 24 runs varying the antecedent runoff condition (ARC) and the initial abstraction for SCS-CN, the initial water content, texture source, spin-up and saturated conductivity (Ks) for GA, and roughness. The SCS-CN peak varied 6- to 12-fold across ARC classes. Conversely, the GA peak varied by only 4% across initial water contents, since crest rainfall exceeded the GA capacity about tenfold, but decreased by 28–77% for a threefold to tenfold Ks, its dominant uncertainty. Despite producing similar overall volumes, the initial discharge peak reached only 2–8% of the main peak under ARC III and 35–44% with the GA spin-up. Additionally, GA reinfiltrated 12–18% of losses as run-on flow, a process absent in SCS-CN. Surface velocities confirmed only crest timing. Thus, a single SCS-CN simulation is not conservative for multi-pulse floods.

papers.title: Ecohydrological trade-offs in revegetation of abandoned coal mines: Soil-water conservation, water cycling and restoration design
Assessing long-term organic manure and superabsorbent polymer benefits for water-limited wheat agriculture through stable water isotope analysis
papers.summary: The soil amendments superabsorbent polymer (SAP) and organic manure (OM) are known to improve soil quality, plant water availability, and crop yields, though soil water processes and mechanisms that underlie these improvements remain unclear. A field experiment of 13 years has been conducted to evaluate the effects of these soil amendments on soil physicochemical properties, aggregate composition, plant photosynthetic properties, and crop yields in a winter wheat agricultural system. Results show that compared with the control, SAP and OM reduced soil bulk density, increased soil organic carbon content and macroaggregate fractions, and effectively improved soil hydraulic properties and water retention capacity. Soil quality improvements were generally greater under OM, but soil moisture levels at the jointing, heading and grain-filling growth stages were greater under SAP. Stable water isotope analysis revealed that SAP and OM enabled plant roots to draw water from deeper soil, and that increased soil moisture under OM and especially SAP was likely due to delayed (not necessarily reduced) evaporative water losses alongside reduced seepage water losses. SAP and OM amendments thereby increased winter wheat population counts, leaf chlorophyll content, net photosynthetic rate, spike grain number, 1000-kernel weight and other yield components, increasing yields in observed years by up to 18.5%. SAP led to annually fluctuating but greater cumulative multi-year yields, whereas OM produced consistent but on average smaller yield improvements over the control. The findings of different long-term effectiveness in improving crop yields and soil quality, and their different underlying mechanisms, enables better-informed evaluations of these amendments.

papers.title: Green-Ampt Infiltration into a Dry Loam: Wetting-Front Suction, Ponding Time and Cumulative Intake Budgets

papers.summary: For a dry loam soil of saturated conductivity 1.4 centimetres per hour, wetting-front suction head twenty centimetres, and moisture deficit 0.25, receiving steady rain at three centimetres per hour, this paper computes a Green-Ampt infiltration and ponding budget. papers.summary: Soil-plant-atmosphere continuum (SPAC) models are commonly used to investigate various components' role(s) in ecosystem functioning. Yet, in most SPAC models, groundwater is ignored or at best represented in an over-simplified manner, leading to misunderstanding of its critical role in simulating soil-vegetation dynamics. This study investigates groundwater's role in SPAC processes, in particular, the impacts of groundwater component (mass and energy) on: (1) regulating the soil profile, in terms of moisture and temperature; (2) the dynamics of the unsaturated/saturated zones and their further impact on water fluxes; and (3) the carbon fluxes and vegetation physiological processes (i.e. root water uptake and photosynthesis reflected by fluorescence). papers.title: Identification of Groundwater Potential Zones Using Remote Sensing and GIS Techniques: A Case Study in Jowhar, Somalia
papers.summary: Abstract Groundwater is the principal source of water supply in Jowhar District, Middle Shabelle Region, Hirshabelle State, Somalia, yet borehole siting has proceeded with limited systematic assessment of the conditions governing its occurrence. This study identified and mapped groundwater potential zones in the district by integrating remote sensing, geographic information systems and the Analytical Hierarchy Process. Nine thematic layers, namely geology, rainfall, soil, drainage density, land use and land cover, slope, lineament density, elevation and the normalized difference vegetation index, were derived from Landsat 8 OLI/TIRS imagery, SRTM digital elevation data, CRU TS rainfall records for 2015 to 2025 and ancillary geological and soil datasets. Each layer was reclassified onto a five-point suitability scale and weighted by pairwise comparison on Saaty's scale. Geology at 26.22 per cent and rainfall at 26.17 per cent emerged as the dominant controls, together accounting for 52.39 per cent of the total weight, with a consistency ratio of 0.038 confirming the acceptability of the judgements. Weighted overlay analysis in ArcGIS produced a groundwater potential index classified into four zones: Good, covering 3,023.99 km² or 67.54 per cent of the district; Moderate, 1,306.52 km² or 29.18 per cent; Poor, 135.22 km² or 3.02 per cent; and Excellent, 11.66 km² or 0.26 per cent. The map was validated against 48 boreholes obtained from the Ministry of Energy and Water Resources of Hirshabelle State and verified in part by field inspection, giving an overall concordance of 47.9 per cent and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.486. Because no borehole lay within the Poor or Excellent zones, two classes remained untested, and the map is accordingly recommended for regional planning rather than for site-specific borehole siting.

papers.source: Journal of Soil Science and Environmental Management

Colonial legacies shape natural hazards in the Atlantic forests of Brazil
papers.summary: Natural hazards pose escalating ecological, public health, and economic challenges globally, with tropical regions bearing a disproportionate burden due to climate change and structural inequalities. This paper examines the intersection of European colonialism, deforestation, and contemporary natural hazard vulnerability in Brazil's Atlantic Forest, one of the world's most biodiverse and threatened biomes. Once covering approximately 15% of Brazilian territory, the Atlantic Forest has been reduced to 24% of its original extent, with only 12.4% comprising mature forest. We argue that the susceptibility of this region to hydrometeorological hazards, particularly flooding, debris flows, and landslides, cannot be understood without reference to the long-term legacies of colonialism, which shaped patterns of land use, urbanization, inequality, and community displacement. Drawing on historical, ecological, and social data, we further demonstrate that Indigenous and Quilombo land management practices offer evidence-based, decolonial pathways to reducing hazard risk and building long-term resilience. We conclude that equitable and effective responses to Anthropocene climate risks in the Global South require explicit engagement with colonial histories as the foundational drivers of contemporary vulnerability.

papers.title: Hydrological controls on deep learning streamflow transferability across contrasting basins
papers.summary: Study region The Yuan River basin, a major tributary of the middle Yangtze River in China, is used as the source basin for model development, and the model's transferability is further evaluated across global hydrological zones. Study focus Accurate streamflow hindcasting using deep learning (DL) is essential for water resources management, yet transferring DL models from local to global scales remains a critical challenge. This study developed a multi-strategy ensemble DL framework that integrates feature selection, time-varying filtering-based empirical mode decomposition, Newton-Raphson-based optimization, and the CNN–BiLSTM–attention network to hindcast daily streamflow and diagnose cross-basin transferability under contrasting hydroclimatic conditions. New hydrological insights for the region In the source basin, the proposed framework achieved robust and statistically consistent improvements over the ML/DL benchmarks. Transfer experiments across 3486 basins showed that the modeling workflow performed most effectively in hydrologically compatible regions, including saturation-excess basins, snowmelt- or permafrost-influenced regimes, and catchments with coherent seasonal runoff patterns. Poor transferability to arid infiltration-excess basins and dryland systems with transmission losses highlights the heterogeneous runoff mechanisms that disrupt rainfall-runoff relationships between source and target basins. These results indicate that cross-basin DL transfer is associated with runoff generation similarity, rainfall spatial organization, regime regularity, and anthropogenic influences, rather than neural architecture alone, thereby informing water resources management across diverse global basins.

papers.title: Hydraulic Response and Microstructural Evolution During Erosional Failure of Spoil Slopes Under Extreme Rainfall
papers.summary: Progressive failure of spoil slopes under extreme rainfall involves multiscale processes, including rainfall infiltration, fine-particle migration, and weakening of the particle skeleton, while their cross-scale evolution remains insufficiently understood. To investigate this mechanism, laboratory model tests were conducted under a rainfall intensity of 108 mm/h with degrees of compaction of 75%, 80%, and 90%. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and PFC2D simulations were further employed to examine failure characteristics at the macroscopic, microstructural, and particle scales. The results show that, at 80% compaction, the slope underwent a progressive sequence of fine-particle migration and toe deposition, erosion-gully development, toe undercutting, and intensified shoulder erosion. Pore-water pressure responses also showed clear spatial differences between the crest, middle slope, and toe. As the degree of compaction increased from 75% to 90%, the maximum deposition length, maximum deposition depth, and dry mass of deposited material decreased by 29.8%, 31.0%, and 38.6%, respectively. SEM observations indicate that increasing compaction generally enhances particle contact and structural integrity, thereby reducing local structural disturbance caused by prolonged rainfall. PFC simulations show that particle displacement is mainly concentrated in the shallow slope, particularly near the shoulder and toe, while the number of bond failures increased from 276 at Step 130 to 3488 at the final failure stage. The experiments and SEM observations provide the basis for comparing compaction levels, whereas the PFC results offer a particle-scale interpretation of progressive failure at 80% compaction. The numerical findings do not establish how particle-scale damage varies with compaction.

papers.title: A comparative study of pond linings for effective water storage in arid and semi-arid regions
papers.summary: Abstract Rainwater harvesting ponds (RWHPs) are increasingly promoted in arid and semi-arid regions to enhance water storage and agricultural resilience amidst erratic rainfall and prolonged dry spells. However, seepage losses remain a major constraint, largely attributable to inadequate lining practices. This study evaluates the field performance and cost-effectiveness of five commonly used lining materials: kaolinite, bitumen, vertisol, an 80 µm-thick polyethylene geomembrane, and masonry riprap, under natural rainfall conditions in Burkina Faso during the 2024 rainy season. A randomized, full-scale field experiment with four replicates was conducted to assess infiltration rates, material behavior over time, and practical construction aspects. Bitumen exhibited the highest water retention performance, reducing seepage by 85%, though it is the most expensive option. Kaolinite represents an optimal trade-off between performance and affordability, reducing infiltration by 82% while remaining substantially more affordable and accessible to rural communities. Vertisol's performance improved mid-season due to clay swelling and natural vegetative cover. In contrast, the geomembrane showed a 10% drop in efficiency due to early degradation, and masonry riprap proved the least effective but exhibited marginal improvement over time. Beyond hydraulic performance, the study also assessed material availability, installation techniques, labour requirements, and environmental considerations. These findings collectively highlight the critical importance of context-specific material selection to optimize RWHP design for effective water storage in resource-constrained settings. By combining technical data with practical insights, this study provides evidence-based recommendations for engineers, practitioners, and policymakers aiming to scale up climate-resilient, cost-effective water storage infrastructure for smallholder farming communities.

papers.title: Mapping soil hydropedological response groups to analyse patterns of observed landslide occurrence at catchment scale in the Eastern Cape province of South Africa
papers.source: South African Journal of Plant and Soil
papers.summary: Landslides are widespread natural hazards, often driven by complex interactions between terrain, hydrology and soil properties. This study investigates the hydropedological characteristics of soils in relation to mapped landslide sites near Port St Johns and Lusikisiki in the Eastern Cape province of South Africa. The Soil-Landscape Inference Model (SoLIM) was used to produce a rule-based digital soil map of Hydropedological Response Groups (HRGs) representing soil–water dynamics across landscape positions. Field-based HRG classification was informed by 186 soil points across dominant land types, complemented by terrain and hydrological covariates. The HRGs map was validated with an overall classification accuracy of 68% and Cohen’s Kappa coefficient of 0.60. Overlay analysis showed that landslide occurrences were predominantly associated with recharge (shallow) and recharge (slow) soil types found on mid- to upper-slope positions with moderate to steep slopes. The study demonstrates that rule-based HRG mapping, when grounded in local soil and terrain understanding, is effective in delineating zones of heightened landslide occurrence. Moreover, it provides a framework for integrating soil hydrology into regional landslide hazard assessments by classifying soils into HRGs. Limitations include potential misclassification due to limited subsoil information and spatial resolution constraints.

papers.title: Groundwater Potential Assessment Using Ann-Rks Machine Learning Based Models in Part of Aule Community, Akure, Nigeria
papers.summary: Abstract This study adopted an integrated approach combining hydrogeological, geophysical, and machine learning techniques to evaluate groundwater potential in Aule Community, Akure, Ondo State, Southwestern Nigeria. Remote sensing data, particularly the ASTER Global Digital Elevation Model (DEM), were processed in ArcMap 10.8.2 to derive key terrain conditioning factors such as slope and aspect, which influence surface runoff, infiltration, and groundwater recharge. The geophysical investigation involved electrical resistivity surveys using the Schlumberger array configuration, with 105 Vertical Electrical Sounding (VES) stations acquired across the study area. Interpretation of the VES data delineated five subsurface geoelectric layers: topsoil, lateritic layer, weathered layer, partially weathered or fractured basement, and fresh basement bedrock, providing detailed insight into aquifer geometry and subsurface conditions. These geoelectric and hydrogeological parameters were integrated as predictor variables within a supervised machine learning framework. A dataset comprising 40 matched well–VES control points were used for model training and validation, with hand-dug well measurements serving as the target variable. Two predictive models were developed: a conventional Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and an enhanced ANN integrated with Random Kitchen Sinks (ANN-RKS) to improve nonlinear feature representation. Using 5-fold cross-validation, the ANN-RKS model outperformed the standard ANN, achieving MAE = 0.056, MSE = 0.006, RMSE = 0.078, and R² = 0.910, compared to MAE = 0.082, MSE = 0.012, RMSE = 0.109, and R² = 0.801 for the ANN model. The optimized ANN-RKS outputs were subsequently spatially interpolated within a GIS environment to generate a detailed groundwater potential map of the study area.

papers.title: Water elevation measurements using sensors for coastal water regions
papers.summary: Water elevation measurements utilizing multispectral, hyperspectral and panchromatic images from satellite, airborne fixed station, mobile platforms and associated in-situ sensing systems is one of the most important geophysical variables needed for calculation of water movement in estuaries, rivers, streams and large water bodies. Often referred to as the stage of the water, the measurement forms the basis for calculating water volume transport, water discharge, and water velocity. The measurement of water elevation is the variable used for expressing flood hazard since water the stage rises there can be impacts upon coastal structure as well as river and shoreline structural integrity. Flood stage prediction is the essential variable used to express coastal flooding hazards. The forcing functions of water stage includes rainfall, runoff, erosion, soil infiltration, floodplain seepage, bottom boundary friction as well as cross-sectional area change. In addition, changes to the water surface slope and capillary waves driven by wind and fetch related variables can influence stage.
