From Competition Release to Ecosystem Functioning: Moderate Thinning Regulates Soil Moisture Availability and Vegetation Responses in Restored Semiarid Caragana microphylla Shrublands of the Loess Plateau, China
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Thinning is widely applied to regulate vegetation density and alleviate competition for soil water availability in restored semiarid shrublands; however, how thinning intensity regulates integrated plant–soil responses and functioning across a thinning gradient remains insufficiently quantified, as previous studies have emphasized vegetation or soil‐water responses rather than their integrated responses to thinning intensity. This study evaluated how thinning intensity regulates vegetation growth, soil moisture, understory vegetation and community composition in Caragana microphylla shrublands in the Anjiapo catchment, Zulihe Watershed, western Loess Plateau, China. Field measurements during the 2024–2026 growing seasons quantified shrub traits, soil moisture, biomass, and understory community attributes under four thinning intensities: control (CT, 0%), light thinning (LT, 20%), moderate thinning (MT, 40%) and heavy thinning (HT, 60%). Moderate thinning produced the strongest responses, with the highest plant height, diameter at stump height, basal area and stem volume. Soil moisture reached its maximum under moderate thinning (11.14% ± 1.55%), accompanied by the highest herbaceous biomass (0.22 ± 0.01 t ha −1 ), shrub biomass (0.24 ± 0.01 t ha −1 ), herb‐layer Shannon diversity (1.66 ± 0.13) and shrub‐layer species richness (8.67 ± 0.66). Thinning significantly altered understory community composition, with moderate thinning showing a distinct community position. These findings suggest that moderate thinning may provide a management strategy for balancing vegetation performance and soil water availability, thereby supporting ecohydrological functioning in restored C. microphylla shrublands.

papers.title: Assessing the impact of soil erosion, flash floods, and sedimentation on Upper Borkena watershed, Awash River Basin, Ethiopia
papers.source: Progress in Physical Geography Earth and Environment
papers.summary: Erosion and sedimentation cause inestimable damage to life and infrastructure in the Awash River Basin. This research assessed the impact of erosion and sediment in the upper Borkena watershed at the Awash River Basin. The assessment was conducted using QSWAT and GIS models to estimate the flood and sediment generated from the watershed. Runoff data were obtained from Borkena station, whereas sediment data were transposed from the nearest station for calibration and validation. Model calibration and uncertainty analysis were performed with sequential uncertainty fitting (SUFI-2), which is one of the programs interfaced with SWAT, in the package SWAT-CUP (SWAT Calibration Uncertainty Programs). Two measures were used to assess the goodness of calibration and uncertainty analysis: (a) the percentage of data bracketed by the 95% prediction uncertainty (95PPU) (P factor), and (b) the ratio of the average thickness of the 95PPU band to the standard deviation of the corresponding measured variable (D factor). Ideally, the P factor tends towards 1, and the D factor is close to zero. These measures together indicate the strength of the calibration-uncertainty analysis. The P factor for Borkena stations was obtained as 0.74, and the D factor was 0.03. These measures indicate a fair model calibration and accounting of uncertainties. The predicted streamflow value at the Borkena River is quite similar to that of the observed discharge. The model performance was checked by three performance parameters, such as goodness of fit (R 2 = 0.73), Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE = 0.62), and percent bias efficiency (PBIAS % = 24.5). The annual observed and simulated flows were 329.51 m 3 /s and 240.37 m 3 /s, respectively. The annual observed and simulated sediment yield was estimated at 480.07 tones/year and 602.79 tones/year. Therefore, soil and water conservation activities have to be strengthened in the study area in the future.

papers.title: BBM-Based Analysis of Settlement Behavior and Pile Reinforcement Performance in an Expansive Soil Embankment
papers.summary: This study investigates the long-term wetting-induced deformation of an unsaturated expansive-soil embankment under seasonal rainfall and drying and evaluates the effects of pile reinforcement. A two-dimensional hydro-mechanical model incorporating the Barcelona Basic Model was implemented in FLAC2D and driven by 473 days of measured daily rainfall. Field vertical displacements at depths of 1.5 and 4.5 m were used to evaluate the untreated section. The model reproduced the main seasonal, cumulative, and time-lagged deformation characteristics, with correlation coefficients of 0.963 and 0.948 at the two monitoring depths. Rainfall infiltration occurred mainly through the exposed slope surface, causing concentrated wetting and settlement near the shoulder–slope transition zone. Within the continuous-strip cases, increasing pile modulus provided only limited additional benefit, whereas increasing pile length more effectively reduced deep settlement. The continuous-strip model predicted greater pavement settlement reduction than the structural-pile model under the adopted modeling assumptions. In the quicklime–cement composite pile-treated section, the equivalent swelling-pile case captured the observed contrast between shallow upward displacement and deeper settlement, suggesting a possible contribution of pile swelling. However, it underestimated shallow uplift and did not reproduce the measured deep-settlement history.

Pore shape and its spatial organization control intrinsic permeability of porous media
papers.summary: The structure of a porous material, and in particular its spatial variability, is known to control the intrinsic permeability of the system. We investigate how dead-end pores influence the intrinsic permeability of a porous medium beyond their contribution to total pore volume. Dead-end pores are ubiquitous in porous media, yet they are often treated as hydraulically inactive regions whose influence is assumed to be negligible or absorbed into effective-porosity descriptions. We perform pore-scale flow simulations across different dead-end pore structures, including heterogeneous arrangements, controlled granular assemblies, and a minimal single-channel model to study their impact on the system macroscopic permeability. This strategy allows us to isolate the effects of dead-end pore density, depth, and orientation while preserving the transmitting network. We find that dead-end pores can influence intrinsic permeability: increasing the density of dead-end pores along percolating flow paths enhances permeability, whereas pore depth and junction orientation have negligible effects. The observed permeability enhancement originates from localized hydrodynamic interactions at junctions between transmitting and dead-end pores. Based on these results, we propose an effective formulation that relates the density and spatial organization of dead-end pores relative to the transmitting network to macroscopic permeability. Our findings show that dead-end pore architecture provides an additional geometric control on intrinsic permeability beyond porosity and pore-size statistics.

Mechanism of shallow hard-shell-layer formation for newly-reclaimed dredged silt using vacuum dewatering combined with preloading
papers.summary: Newly-reclaimed dredged silt sites present a critical geotechnical challenge immediately after hydraulic filling. The ground surface remains as fluidized mud, preventing personnel and equipment access, yet conventional treatment methods assume the site is already accessible. This paper proposes a vacuum dewatering combined with preloading (VDCP) method for rapid formation of a shallow hard-shell layer without sand cushions or prolonged drying. A three-dimensional horizontal–vertical drainage network is established, coupling free-water extraction and negative-pressure consolidation. Physical model tests on Xiamen dredged silt (initial water content 281%) and Plaxis 2D numerical simulations are conducted to investigate the reinforcement mechanisms during the hard-shell formation stage. After 1,188 h of vacuum extraction, the average water content of the shallow soil decreases to 58%, the void ratio reduces from 7.53 to 1.49, and the ultimate bearing capacity increases from near zero to over 40 kPa, meeting the requirements for personnel and light machinery access. Numerical comparisons demonstrate that the three-dimensional drainage system achieves approximately 61.0% excess pore water pressure dissipation within 1,200 h, compared with 22.4% for horizontal-only and 18.3% for vertical-only drainage, confirming the synergistic effect of combined drainage channels, although these ratios are semi-quantitative. A consolidation coupling effect between vacuum and surcharge is observed; however, surcharge should be applied only after the soil has gained sufficient shear strength. The VDCP method and the proposed phased treatment framework, which designates shallow hard-shell formation as an independent preliminary stage with explicit transition criteria, provide a feasible technical pathway for similar projects that require priority construction of working platforms before deep reinforcement.

papers.summary: AOSTRA Underground Test Facility (UTF) Phase A is recognized as the birthplace of the Steam Assisted Gravity Drainage (SAGD) process. A typical SAGD project consists of a horizontal injection well drilled approximately 5 m above a horizontal production well. The process concept relies on a continuous injection of high temperature steam that forms a steam chamber to heat up the viscous oil and make it mobile. The UTF Phase A pilot introduces the concept of shaft and tunnel access by constructing two shafts to a depth of 220 m and a 1.5 km long tunnel. The pilot consists of three horizontal well pairs that were drilled upward from the tunnel, each with an approximately 60 m horizontal completion section in the oil sands reservoir. The monitoring program at UTF Phase A provided unprecedented insights into the mechanism and formation response associated with the SAGD process. papers.title: Prioritizing Fuel Treatments to Reduce Post-Fire Debris Flow Risk in Utah
papers.summary: Wildfire is a natural part of many forest ecosystems, but in the western United States, wildfires have become larger, more frequent, and more severe in recent decades. There are serious problems after severe wildfire, including erosion, flooding, and debris flows that threaten water quality, roads, and communities. Because of this, land managers need better ways to decide where fuel treatments, such as prescribed burning or thinning, can most effectively reduce wildfire damage and post-fire risks. In this dissertation, I studied how fuel treatments might reduce wildfire severity and lower the risk of post-fire debris flows in Utah. First, I built a model to predict how severely forests are likely to burn across the state. Next, I used simulated treatment scenarios to test how different fuel treatments changed wildfire severity in different forest types and under different weather conditions. Finally, I applied those results to real watersheds in Utah to estimate how treatments could reduce post-fire debris-flow risk. papers.summary: Infrastructure earthworks require soils with adequate strength, manageable deformation and suitable hydraulic behaviour. Conventional stabilisation with cement and lime can achieve these requirements, but their manufacture has substantial negative environmental effects. Biopolymers offer a potential means of reducing reliance on conventional binders, but their performance is often assessed through strength tests under partially saturated conditions. Their behaviour in saturated and/or near-saturated conditions, effects on compressibility and drainage, and the benefits of combining them with a traditional stabiliser like hydrated lime remain insufficiently understood. This study addresses these gaps to establish when biopolymer-hydrated lime treatment can provide useful soil improvement. An experimental programme investigated London clay, Ligurian sandy silt, pyroclastic silty sand and Karlsruhe fine sand. Treatment of these soils with Guar gum (GG), xanthan gum (XG) and agar gum (AG) was examined either alone or as partial replacements for hydrated lime (HL), at a fixed total stabiliser content of 3% of dry soil mass. Atterberg limits and standard Proctor tests characterised London clay consistency and compaction; oedometer, evaporation and direct shear tests examined the hydromechanical responses of the coarser soils. Saturated consolidated drained triaxial tests further assessed untreated, HL-treated and AG-containing Karlsruhe fine sand under effective confining stresses of 100, 300 and 600 kPa. papers.title: Longitudinal Dynamic Response of End-Bearing Piles in Radially Heterogeneous Unsaturated Soil
papers.summary: This study investigates the longitudinal dynamic response of end-bearing piles embedded in radially heterogeneous unsaturated soil induced by construction disturbance. The unsaturated soil is described using the theory of motion for three-phase poroelastic media, while the radial inhomogeneity of the surrounding soil is represented by the complex shear stiffness transfer model. The soil is discretized into concentric vertical annular zones, each of which is assumed to be homogeneous, while soil properties may differ between adjacent zones. The governing equations for each soil zone are then solved and coupled with the pile governing equation to derive an analytical solution for the pile-head complex impedance. After validating the proposed solution, a parametric analysis is conducted to examine how pile–soil parameters affect the longitudinal dynamic response of end-bearing piles in radially heterogeneous unsaturated soil.

papers.summary: Compacted clays are widely used in road embankments, railway subgrades, levees, and many other infrastructure projects. In regions such as Alberta, compacted clay fills are subjected to long-term loading and seasonal moisture variations, which may result in creep deformation and long-term settlement, posing challenges to infrastructure serviceability. Previous studies on creep behaviour of cohesive soils have mainly focused on saturated soils, whereas research on compacted unsaturated fine-grained soils remains limited. Further, creep studies of unsaturated clay in the literature are characterized by relatively short testing durations ranging from several days to one or two weeks. Longer durations are required to obtain reliable results to guide practice. In this study, long-duration creep tests were conducted on two types of compacted soils obtained from Edmonton, including a low- to intermediate-plasticity clay (classification CL–CI) and a high-plasticity clay (CH). The effects of stress level, relative compaction, soil plasticity, initial water content and moisture change on the long-term deformation behaviour of compacted unsaturated soils were investigated. In addition, consolidation behaviour under saturated conditions was compared with the unsaturated creep behaviour. Vertical stresses ranging from 50 to 400 kPa were applied during the long-duration creep tests, which were performed under sealed high-humidity conditions with a relatively constant temperature of approximately 20 ℃ and relative humidity exceeding 99%. Test durations ranged from approximately 3 to 11 weeks, substantially longer than those commonly reported in previous creep studies of unsaturated clays. Under unsaturated conditions, both the CL–CI and CH soils exhibited continuous creep deformation accompanied by water uptake during long-term loading, with equilibrium water contents ranging from approximately 19% to 23% for the CL–CI soil and 28% to 38% for the CH soil. papers.title: An analytical, single parameter model of falling-head ponded infiltration
papers.summary: In this study, an analytical model is developed of the water-level dynamics of a temporary surface pond formed by sudden flooding of initially unsaturated soil. Pond-depth evolution is governed by infiltration and a constant evaporation rate. The model couples a surface-water balance equation with a linearized Richards equation, assuming constant hydraulic conductivity and specific moisture capacity. Although subsurface water transport is described by conventional Fickian diffusion, the coupling introduces a temporal memory kernel into the reduced equation governing pond depth, giving rise to effective non-Fickian relaxation dynamics. The resulting semi-infinite analytical solution is expressed in terms of the scaled complementary error function, which corresponds to a fractional relaxation function with an algebraic asymptote. The solution also allows the characteristic pond-emptying time to be determined. The analytical model is evaluated against numerical integration of the nonlinear Richards equation using van Genuchten–Mualem hydraulic properties of sandy loam, loam, and clay loam soils. The model reproduces the simulated pond-depth evolution with good accuracy ($R^2 > 0.95$ in all investigated cases). For hydrostatic initial conditions, only the product of hydraulic conductivity and specific moisture capacity is identifiable. The fitted parameter decreases systematically with groundwater table depth, following an approximate power-law scaling relationship with the initial pressure-head difference. The overall results demonstrate how effective non-Fickian dynamics can emerge from coupled Fickian transport processes and provide a computationally inexpensive description of nonlinear infiltration dynamics

papers.title: Estimation and Modeling of Groundwater Contaminants in Uttarakhand's state
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: The Himalayan State of Uttarakhand in northern India relies heavily on groundwater to meet the drinking water and agricultural needs. However, rapid urbanization, industrial activities, and irrigation practices have led to increased contamination of groundwater resources. The quality of both surface water and groundwater in Uttarakhand is deteriorating due to developmental activities, geological factors, and the mixing of industrial wastes. The harmful toxic metal ions such as arsenic, cadmium, chromium, and lead have been detected in drinking water sources across most districts of the state. Among these contaminants, lead has been found to be detrimental to health health. Lead, a potent neurotoxin, poses severe health risks, especially through contaminated drinking water and food. In children, lead exposure can cause cognitive impairment, learning disabilities, and behavioral disorders, while in adults, prolonged exposure increases the risk of hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, kidney damage, and reproductive complications. The movement of lead in regional groundwater systems occurs through unsaturated porous media, where preferential flow pathways significantly influence the distribution of soil water content and solute concentrations. The toxicological effects of lead ions have been assessed through laboratory experiments based on the stipulated limits recommended by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) and the World Health Organization (WHO). To better understand the extent of lead contamination, this study numerically develops regional transport models to estimate the movement of lead contaminants in both spatial and temporal domains. The findings aim to provide insights into the transport dynamics of lead in groundwater and support the formulation of effective mitigation strategies for safeguarding water quality in Uttarakhand.

Graph‐Based Automated Discovery of Concise Soil Hydraulic Functions From Data: Beyond Empirical Formulations
papers.summary: Abstract Soil hydraulic functions underpin water flow and transport modeling in the vadose zone, yet they are commonly represented by expert‐designed formulations such as the Mualem–van Genuchten (MvG) model. Because these formulations rest on predefined functional assumptions, balancing predictive accuracy and parametric compactness across soil textures remains challenging. Here we introduce a graph‐based equation discovery framework that distills soil hydraulic functions from experimental data. Reapplied to the original data sets that motivated the MvG parameterization, the framework recovers a concise water retention function together with an analytical unsaturated hydraulic conductivity expression whose mathematical structure departs from classical empirical forms. Evaluated across soils of contrasting texture, the discovered model predicts unsaturated hydraulic conductivity more accurately than MvG and its common variants, while its fitted parameters retain interpretable correlations with measurable soil physical properties. These findings suggest that data‐driven discovery can yield compact, analytically tractable constitutive relations that move beyond fixed empirical formulations.

papers.title: Stability analysis of ultra-high arch dams under temperature-stress coupling and cumulative temperature damage
papers.summary: In the high-altitude regions of southwestern China, large diurnal and annual temperature fluctuations impose substantial thermal loads on ultra-high arch dams. Given their marked sensitivity to thermal variations, these structures face considerable threats to their safety and stability. To investigate the coupling effect between the temperature and stress fields of the dam body under high‑altitude and large temperature difference conditions, and to assess the influence of cumulative thermal damage on the structural response of the arch dam, this study takes a 217 m high asymmetric double curvature concrete arch dam as the research object. A thermo‑mechanical coupled numerical model is established using the ANSYS finite element method, incorporating self‑weight, hydrostatic pressure, silt pressure, and thermal loads. The displacement and stress field distributions of the dam under two operating conditions—sudden temperature rise and sudden temperature drop at normal storage level—are comparatively analyzed. The results indicate that the total displacement on the upstream face exhibits a symmetrical arc‑shaped distribution centered at the crown of the dam crest. It slightly increases under cooling and slightly decreases under warming, with magnitudes remaining within the normal elastic range. A temperature decrease causes the dam crest to deflect downstream, whereas a temperature increase causes it to deflect upstream. In the direction perpendicular to the river channel, significant torsional deformation is observed due to thermal regulation: clockwise torsion under cooling and counterclockwise torsion under warming, with consistent deformation patterns on both upstream and downstream faces. Under the cooling condition, compressive stresses dominate in the dam body, with tensile stress concentration occurring at the upstream arch abutments. Soil temperature, water content, soil moisture characteristic curve, total porosity, and water-stable aggregates were measured. The results showed that the temperature change in the surface soil was the most severe, and it gradually weakened with an increase in soil depth. The temperature change pattern of the paddy field soil was basically consistent with that of the dry field soil. During the freeze–thaw period, the soil temperature in paddy fields was lower than in dry fields, while during the crop growth period, the soil temperature in the paddy fields was higher than that in the dry fields. Overall, the soil water content gradually increases from the surface to the bottom layer. The soil moisture characteristic curves of each representative station show similar trends in each suction stage. The soil moisture characteristic curve of the Sanjiang Plain shows less water loss in the low suction stage, while the high suction stage has more water loss. The soil moisture characteristic curve of the Songnen Plain shows more water loss in the low suction stage than in the Sanjiang Plain. In the low suction stage, the water loss of paddy soil is similar to that of dry field soil, while in the high suction stage, the water loss is greater than that of dry field soil. Therefore, the water storage capacity of dry field soil is better. The total porosity of soil gradually decreases with an increase in soil depth, and the total porosity of paddy field soil is greater than that of dry field soil. papers.title: A Strain-Driven PINN Incorporating Constitutive Models for Unsaturated Soils
papers.summary: The hydraulic and mechanical properties of unsaturated soils are relatively complex. To address the highly nonlinear hydro-mechanical behavior of unsaturated soils, this study proposes a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) model constrained by the constitutive model of unsaturated soils. Driven by axial strain, the model uses a fully connected neural network to predict five variables, including axial stress, suction, effective saturation, void ratio and confining pressure. The constitutive relationships of soil-water characteristic curves, and boundary conditions are all embedded in the loss function to ensure that the predictions comply with physical laws. The model was validated by using unsaturated triaxial test data under various overconsolidation ratios and suction conditions. Sensitivity analysis indicated that λ = 0.1 yielded the lowest combined error among the candidate weights examined, indicating a high agreement between the predicted results and experimental data. The established model can reproduce the deviator stress and volumetric changes in unsaturated expansive soil under different stress histories, and the model demonstrates promising prediction performance across the investigated strain stages under the available triaxial test conditions. Comparisons with the MLP baseline and a conventional constitutive model indicate that the proposed PINN can reproduce the main trends in the investigated hydro-mechanical responses.

papers.title: Experimental and numerical assessment of calcium hydroxide dosage on the seepage performance of Yellow River sediment-based alkali-activated materials for embankment seepage control
papers.summary: To investigate the effect of calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)2) dosage on the seepage performance of Yellow River sediment-based alkali-activated materials, Yellow River sediment from the Huayuankou reach was used as the main precursor in a composite NaOH-Ca(OH)2 activation system. The permeability coefficient was systematically examined at Ca(OH)2 dosages of 2.5%-15.0% (by mass of dry sediment) and curing ages of 3, 7, and 28 days, and low-field nuclear magnetic resonance (LF-NMR) was used to characterize the pore structure and its relationship with permeability. The permeability coefficient exhibited a pronounced nonlinear response to Ca(OH)2 dosage. Increasing the dosage from 2.5% to 10.0% reduced the permeability coefficient by 82.58%, 82.45%, and 69.07% at 3, 7, and 28 days, respectively, whereas a further increase to 12.5% caused a rebound of 43.48%, 48.70%, and 13.80%; beyond 12.5%, the permeability decreased again. The small-pore fractal dimension correlated negatively and significantly with the permeability coefficient (R² = 0.92, 0.96, and 0.92 at 3, 7, and 28 days), and a multivariate model linking permeability coefficient, Ca(OH)2 dosage, and curing age was established with R² = 0.97. Two-dimensional seepage analyses of a typical Yellow River embankment (7.02 m high) using GEO-Studio show that, relative to the unreinforced embankment, reinforcement layers prepared with 10.0% and 12.5% Ca(OH)2 lowered the elevation of the seepage exit point from 33.45 m to 33.30 m and 33.27 m (i.e., by 0.15 m and 0.18 m), while the unit-width seepage discharge remained almost unchanged (from 6.14 × 10 ⁻ ⁷ to 6.89 × 10 ⁻ ⁷ and 6.95 × 10 ⁻ ⁷ m³/(s·m)). This indicates a redistribution of the seepage field and a lower phreatic surface, rather than a deterioration in impermeability. The results provide a reference for the resource utilization of Yellow River sediment in embankment seepage control.

papers.summary: This study delves into the early warning system for regional rainfall-induced landslide hazards. By integrating landslide susceptibility mapping and critical rainfall thresholds, a spatiotemporal probabilistic prediction framework for landslide hazards is established. Taking Wushan County as the study area, the authors utilised 313 recorded rainfall-triggered landslide events and meteorological rainfall data spanning from 2010 to 2024. Initially, a landslide susceptibility prediction model was constructed using the Random Forest algorithm, with model accuracy validated by the area under the curve (AUC) metric (AUC = 0.85). Subsequently, critical rainfall thresholds were determined through a comprehensive analysis of antecedent effective rainfall, employing three models: effective rainfall intensity-duration (EI-D), cumulative effective rainfall-duration (EE-D), and cumulative effective rainfall-effective rainfall intensity (EE-EI). Finally, a landslide hazard warning map was generated by spatially superimposing susceptibility classifications and rainfall threshold exceedance probabilities, accompanied by corresponding disaster prevention strategies. The results demonstrate that this integrated methodology enhances the precision of regional landslide early warnings, as supported by quantitative validation metrics (probability of detection = 0.76, true skill statistic = 0.44), providing a scientifically robust decision making framework for natural resource management authorities in disaster risk mitigation.

papers.summary: Higher overall accuracy does not necessarily mean more complete landslide mapping at every location. Across eight rainfall-related events, we examine the benefits of earlier satellite imagery using U-TAE, a neural network that combines images acquired on different dates, as the main model. We compare overall accuracy with the fraction of mapped landslide area detected within local image patches. Mean average precision increased from 0.333 with a post-event image to 0.379 with a pre/post pair and 0.419 with a longer sequence. Adding earlier images to the pair improved mean average precision in seven events but slightly reduced it in Chimanimani. However, the average increase in the detected fraction across locations and regions was 1.1 percentage points (95% interval −1.3 to +3.3). This provides no clear evidence that earlier images increased the average fraction of mapped landslide area detected. The estimated gain in Italy decreased from 3.0 to 0.3 percentage points when the decision thresholds changed, indicating that the apparent improvement depended on how the predictions were converted into a landslide map. The benefit of earlier images was also greater in patches containing more mapped landslide area in some regions, but was not clearly related to the strength of surface change in patches with sufficient mapped area and usable optical observations. An auxiliary comparison with U-Net, a convolutional image-segmentation model, also showed local detection differences alongside higher overall accuracy. Local detection also varied when the same models were retrained using unchanged images. Checking local detection changes alongside conventional accuracy measures helps assess whether adding earlier imagery reduces missed landslide area across locations.

papers.summary: Abstract Separated analyses are widely used to evaluate the stability of slopes after rainfall and earthquakes. However, the combined impact of rainfall infiltration and earthquake shaking on slope stability remains insufficiently studied. Therefore, a unique closed-form analytical solution to calculate the factor of safety (FS) for homogeneous unsaturated slopes under combined seepage and seismic forces has been proposed by modifying the conventional Bishop’s method. The two-dimensional seepage pattern was considered to capture rainfall infiltration, while pseudo-dynamic forces at each failure slice accounted for earthquake shaking. Further, an analytical search method was developed to locate the critical slip surface. Additionally, a coupled hydromechanical finite-element model was used to analyze rainfall-induced seepage, deformation, and stress redistribution. The resulting slope condition was further evaluated under seismic loading to represent rainfall–earthquake effects without implying full two-way coupling between infiltration and earthquake shaking. All these newly proposed methodologies were applied to the 2014 Malin landslide in Maharashtra, India, to replicate the landslide mechanism and identify root causes to show the application of proposed analytical solutions. A comparison with field observations and literature demonstrated that both the analytical and numerical models realistically represented the Malin landslide. Further, the proposed analytical model was validated against a numerical analysis of a real earthquake-induced landslide. The models accurately reproduced the onset, failure zone, and progression of instability over time. The present study provides the application of new analytical solutions for practical landslides, additionally offering a reference for prevention and evacuation plans.

papers.title: Seismic–Tectonic Predictors of Landslide Susceptibility in the Western Himalayas: A Spatially Validated Machine Learning Assessment
papers.summary: Seismicity may contribute to regional slope instability in the Western Himalayas, but its incremental predictive value relative to a matched non-seismic baseline remains poorly quantified. This study assessed the regional contribution of seismic–tectonic predictors using 763 geocoded NASA Global Landslide Catalog reports from 2007–2017, 345 earthquakes of magnitude 5.5–7.6 from 1965–2016, mapped active faults, and hydrographic variables. Landslides were aggregated to a 0.25° grid, yielding 231 presence cells among 1,600 cells. Spatial block-permutation tests, nested five-fold spatial cross-validation, four classifiers, matched baseline comparisons, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were applied. Landslide-presence cells were closer to catalogued earthquakes than background cells (61.5 vs. 118.3 km; P = 0.0005) and had a higher energy-weighted seismicity index (2.323 vs. 2.003; P = 0.0015). Random forest achieved the strongest mean discrimination and calibration (ROC–AUC = 0.855 ± 0.027; PR–AUC = 0.489 ± 0.073; Brier score = 0.096 ± 0.004). Adding seismic–tectonic predictors increased random-forest ROC–AUC by 0.048 and reduced the Brier score by 0.014, although paired tests across five folds did not reach P < 0.05. The high and very high susceptibility classes occupied 16.5% of grid cells and contained 68.2% of catalogued events. Earthquake proximity, Gaussian earthquake density, and energy-weighted seismicity were the leading physical seismic predictors in SHAP analysis. These findings indicate useful regional seismic–tectonic predictive information but do not establish earthquake triggering or causation. Interpretation is limited by catalogue reporting bias, coarse mapping units, mixed magnitude scales, and unavailable terrain variables.

papers.summary: The Karakoram Highway (KKH) traverses a tectonically active and climatically sensitive mountain corridor that is repeatedly affected by landslides. This study develops an integrated hybrid framework combining convolutional neural network–long short-term memory (CNN-LSTM) learning, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), persistent-scatterer interferometric synthetic aperture radar (PS-InSAR), runout modelling, climate projections, and multi-hazard risk assessment along a 320-km section of the KKH in northwestern Pakistan. Eighteen topographic, hydrological, geological, climatic, anthropogenic, and geodetic conditioning factors were used. The CNN-LSTM was pre-trained on the NASA Cooperative Open Online Landslide Repository and fine-tuned using an inventory of 612 landslides, while class imbalance was addressed using SMOTE and focal loss. The stacked hybrid model achieved an AUC of 0.974, accuracy of 0.928, and Cohen’s κ of 0.856, outperforming standalone CNN-LSTM (AUC = 0.951) and XGBoost (AUC = 0.938) models. SHAP and Grad-CAM analyses identified slope, PS-InSAR line-of-sight velocity, annual rainfall, and elevation as the dominant controls. Flow-R and RAMMS simulations reproduced representative runout patterns with κ = 0.74. Under CMIP6 SSP5-8.5, high-to-very-high susceptibility is projected to increase from 24.0% at baseline to 35.2% by 2050 and 41.6% by 2100. The multi-hazard assessment further indicates that 23.7% of the highway lies within high-to-very-high composite risk zones. The framework provides an explainable, climate-sensitive, and operationally transferable basis for landslide-risk reduction along high-relief transport corridors.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards, causing substantial loss of life and infrastructure, particularly in mountainous regions. Accurate identification of landslide-prone areas remains challenging due to complex and nonlinear interactions among geological, topographical, and environmental factors. This study evaluates kernel-based machine learning approaches, namely, kernel logistic regression (KLR) and support vector machine (SVM), for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) in Sikkim, India. A balanced data set comprising 693 landslide and 695 nonlandslide samples was constructed using 15 conditioning factors representing topographic, hydrological, environmental, geological, and seismic conditions. The grid search method was utilized to identify optimal hyperparameter configurations. Model performance was quantitatively assessed using accuracy, kappa coefficient, specificity, area under curve (AUC), landslide density, and success rate curve (SRC). The results demonstrate that the KLR with a polynomial kernel (KLR_poly) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.741 and an area under curve (AUC) of 0.829, outperforming other KLR variants, while the SVM with an rbf kernel (SVM_rbf) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.749 and an AUC of 0.764, outperforming other SVM variants. Furthermore, the landslide density analysis showed a systematic increase in landslide concentration from low to high susceptibility classes for nonlinear models, while SRC results indicated moderate to good predictive capability across all models, confirming effective spatial prioritization of landslide-prone areas. Additionally, a feature importance analysis was conducted to identify the most significant factors influencing landslide occurrence.

papers.summary: Abstract The region of Muzaffarabad, located in the tectonically active foothills of the Himalayas, is highly vulnerable to landslides due to frequent slope failures exacerbated by both natural and anthropogenic factors. This study assesses landslide susceptibility and hazard in Muzaffarabad, Azad Jammu and Kashmir, Pakistan, using two machine learning (ML) approaches, specifically Logistic Regression (LR) and Random Forest (RF). A total of thirteen landslide conditioning factors, including topographic, geological, environmental and anthropogenic attributes, were analyzed using models. Landslide susceptibility maps were developed and validated with landslide datasets from 2005, 2007, and 2012, showcasing the models’ predictive performance through accuracy metrics such as Area Under Curve (AUC), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), F1-score and Kappa. The study found that RF models consistently outperformed LR models in predictive accuracy, with AUC values of 99% for the 2007 dataset and 96.3% for the 2012 dataset. Temporal validation of these models against subsequent-year landslide inventories demonstrated that RF retained stronger predictive stability over time than LR, although the use of static conditioning layers limits the interpretation of these temporal changes as direct evidence of landscape dynamics. The results underscore the potential of RF-based models for operational landslide hazard assessments, providing critical insights for hazard mitigation and urban planning in tectonically active regions. The study’s findings contribute to the development of more effective risk management strategies, particularly in the face of ongoing seismic activity and climate change, enhancing regional resilience to landslide disasters.

papers.summary: Landslides are one of the most destructive natural hazards. In highway construction, cut slopes are particularly prone to instability and failure because excavation disturbs the original stress state. Monitoring slope stability and issuing early warnings can effectively prevent casualties and mitigate losses. Traditional slope monitoring relies mainly on surface displacement and other external deformation measurements, which are relatively insensitive to internal damage preceding visible failure. In this study, we conducted a monitoring experiment on a cut slope in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, using ambient noise interferometry, which provides a continuous, non-invasive means of monitoring relative seismic velocity changes (dv/v) that reflect the internal stiffness state of the slope. Velocity changes were obtained by stacking long-duration cross-correlations of ambient noise. However, frequent rainfall severely degraded the reconstruction of Green’s functions from such cross-correlations. To address this issue, we propose a sparse non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) method to suppress rainfall-induced noise and obtain more stable Green’s functions for high-resolution dv/v measurements. The obtained dv/v series exhibited a clear 24 h periodicity consistent with temperature variations, and the seismic velocity decreased by approximately 6% from 9 to 10 August, coinciding with typhoon landfall and heavy rainfall on 9 August. Following the drop in velocity, the inclinometer of the three-component geophone recorded a noticeable slip, and the agreement among the velocity drop, the slip, and field-observed cracks indicates that velocity variations retrieved from ambient noise can effectively reflect the internal stiffness weakening of the cut slope. By integrating the proposed method with other deformation measurements, landslide early warning for cut slopes can be improved.

Goaf and mining blasting represent typical artificial disturbances that affect mine slopes. This paper focuses on the Jiweishan landslide in Wulong, Chongqing, as the primary case study. Through comprehensive geological investigation, numerical simulation, and theoretical analysis, the landslide disaster mechanism influenced by the combined effects of goaf and mining blasting was systematically examined. In this study, UDEC software was used to reveal the failure mechanism of Jiweishan landslide under the combined effects of goaf and mining blasting by using the global block discrete element method in the numerical model. Following the formation of extensive goaf areas from mining, the overlying strata lost support, resulting in uneven settlement. The potential sliding mass tended to experience slight subsidence and lateral deformation. The prescribed blasting input promoted progressive failure in the excavated slope model. Under the given blasting wave input, the Jiweishan landslide exhibited a progressive advancing failure trend: tensile fractures first initiated and developed at the trailing edge of the landslide. As the blasting process continued, the fractures at the rear edge expanded, extended, and connected, whereas the anti-sliding performance of the front-edge locking section progressively deteriorated. Ultimately, the entire front-edge sliding mass was sheared off, resulting in a debris flow disaster. The findings inform sustainable mining practice by highlighting the need to account for goaf-induced deformation in pre-blast slope assessments and by identifying priorities for long-term monitoring, including crack opening at the rear and displacement in the middle and at the front locking segment.

This study employed numerical simulations to investigate the impacts of rainfall infiltration on groundwater seepage under the effect of urban construction. A numerical model was established to predict groundwater level (GWL) in the phreatic aquifer (Aq0), incorporating the actual distribution of impervious surfaces and subsurface structures for a representative urban area in Shanghai. The model accounted for land surface conditions through rainfall infiltration coefficients, while subsurface structures were parameterized using equivalent hydraulic conductivity ( K eq ) derived from effective medium theory. Validation results show that the model achieved a maximum error of only 1.7%, demonstrating reliable performance in predicting groundwater seepage. There is 23.23% area with GWL declining more than 0.4 m in the actual scenario with 93% impervious surface hardening comparing without surface hardening. Prediction scenarios with varying reduction rates of impervious surface compared with the actual scenario ( R a ) were conducted to investigate the impact of surface hardening on GWL. The results indicate average GWL of the study area presents exponential decay with the impervious surface ratio. Further, the variations in GWL of Aq0 were investigated by reducing hardened surfaces in different locations with the same R a . As the proportion of underground structures in the reduced impervious surface increases, the area with the same increment of GWL decreases. Prioritizing low impact development in areas with lower subsurface structure density can significantly enhance the efficiency of groundwater recharge by rainfall infiltration.

This study evaluates two widely used QPE products, Stage IV and the Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) system at 1-km and 4-km spatial resolutions over Puerto Rico using hourly rain gauge observations from October 2020 to November 2023. A distance-based IDW method was applied to extract QPE values at gauge locations, and its sensitivity relative to conventional nearest-pixel matching was evaluated. The evaluation encompassed both unconditional and percentile-based conditional assessments across four precipitation intensity categories (light, moderate, heavy, and extreme) and six geographic regions. Results show that MRMS-1km consistently outperforms Stage IV and MRMS-4km across most metrics, with higher Pearson correlation coefficients (PCC) and lower root mean square error (RMSE), particularly for moderate to extreme precipitation. Geographically weighted regression (GWR) analysis reveals spatially heterogeneous distance–error relationships, most pronounced for MRMS-1km over the central mountainous region. These findings provide actionable guidance for QPE product selection in hydrologic applications and highlight priority areas for targeted gauge-based correction in complex tropical island terrain.

papers.summary: Abstract Introduction Soil erosion threatens land resources, yet splash erosion, its initial stage, remains insufficiently studied. Objectives This study evaluates the effects of cyanobacterial inoculation on splash erosion and soil stability under two salinity–slope settings: lower salinity at a 10% slope and higher salinity at a 5% slope. Methods Triplicate experimental plots were established using soils from two salinity–slope settings and randomly assigned to cyanobacterial inoculation or untreated control treatments. We uniformly applied cultivated, extracted, and propagated cyanobacteria to the soil surface, then incubated the plots for 60 days under controlled conditions. Splash erosion was subsequently simulated using a rainfall simulator under specified intensity and duration, with splash gutters installed on both sides of each plot to collect eroded soil. Soil loss was quantified, and soil stability was evaluated before rainfall simulation. Results Cyanobacterial inoculation reduced mean total splash erosion in both settings, from 1.693 to 0.565 g/m 2 under lower salinity and 10% slope, and from 0.727 to 0.329 g/m 2 under higher salinity and 5% slope. Welch's t tests indicated statistically significant treatment differences ( p = 0.0441 and p = 0.0025, respectively). Mean soil‐stability indices also increased following inoculation, from 1.573 to 7.374 and from 2.006 to 6.929, respectively; however, these differences did not reach statistical significance ( p = 0.0516 and p = 0.0703). Conclusions Cyanobacterial inoculation consistently reduced splash erosion across salinity–slope settings, showing promise as a bio‐based soil stabilizer. Larger experiments are needed to confirm these effects and support reliable restoration.

Additionally, a comprehensive parametric study has been conducted to evaluate the effects of transient flow and elevated temperature on the uplift capacity of shallow strip plate anchors. The results indicate that the behavior of plate anchors in unsaturated sand and silt is distinctly different from that in clay.

papers.summary: Abstract The paper focuses on the effect of the vertical ground acceleration component on slope stability. The proposed stability method is based on Newmark’s sliding block concept, which provides an intuitive indicator of slope stability. Contrary to the original Newmark method, both components of excitations, tangent and normal to the slip plane, are considered in force equilibrium. In the paper, the extended Newmark method is coupled with dynamic response obtained using the FEM and a direct time-integration scheme. Coupling the simple stability approach with the stress distribution history eliminates uncertainty in determining the intensity of the dynamic load acting on the sliding block. In the coupled method, the equilibrium of the sliding and resisting forces is considered along the discretized slip plane. When the limit equilibrium is reached, the relative movement of the block begins, and the permanent displacement of a sliding mass is accumulated. The influence of excitation components on permanent displacement is examined using a uniform steep slope as an example. The presented results indicate that shallow deformation mechanisms are more strongly affected by inertial forces than deeper ones. In the analyzed cases, the peak average acceleration for the shallow mechanism was between 1.2 and 3.0 times that for the deep mechanism. Furthermore, the effect of vertical acceleration on permanent displacements is notably more significant in shallow failure modes. It is shown that the permanent displacement obtained by the original Newmark’s method can be 74.3% lower than that obtained by the extended Newmark’s method. The impact of vertical acceleration itself can reach 24.6%.

papers.summary: Blast-induced ground vibrations in surface mining threaten nearby structures and open-pit slope stability. At the Koidu Mine in Sierra Leone, evidence-based mitigation is needed to protect community infrastructure while preserving slope integrity. This study evaluates the effectiveness of trenching in reducing vibration transmission using numerical simulations in ANSYS LS-DYNA. Four trench depths (0, 10, 16, and 22 m) are assessed against a fixed blast depth of 15 m. The baseline no-trench scenario yielded a peak particle velocity (PPV) of 7.94 mm/s at the nearest surface structure (50 m from the blasthole), below the USBM RI 8507 limit of 12.7 mm/s but exceeding the stricter DIN 4150−3 guideline of 5 mm/s for sensitive structures. Trenching reduced PPV by 46%, 62%, and 66% at depths of 10, 16, and 22 m, respectively, with 16 m identified as the effective optimum due to diminishing returns. These reductions improve foundation-level vibration safety for surface buildings. In contrast, slope stability analyses performed under undrained conditions with the blast vibration applied as a dynamic load showed that the Factor of Safety (FoS) remained below 1.0 in all trench configurations (0.101–0.105). Trench depth therefore had no practical influence on slope stability: the slope failed under blast loading at every depth tested, and the critical PPV threshold lies below the lowest value examined (2.68 mm/s). Consequently, while trenching remains effective for mitigating structural vibration, it is insufficient to guarantee slope stability. An integrated approach combining trenching with drainage systems, ground improvement techniques, or adjusted blast charge designs is therefore required for effective risk management at the Koidu Mine.

The model considers not only the influence of the degree of saturation and viscoplastic strain on soil hardening but also that of viscous volumetric strain on the soil-water characteristic curve. The model could completely describe creep, soil-water characteristics, and mechanical properties of unsaturated soil. papers.summary: Soil–structure interface shear behavior plays a fundamental role in the mechanical stability and hydraulic integrity of geotechnical systems, particularly in expansive soils susceptible to desiccation cracking, curling, and permeability changes during seasonal drying. Direct shear testing is widely used to characterize interface behavior; however, conventional configurations often fail to reproduce the coupled hydro-mechanical and thermal conditions associated with drying and restrained shrinkage. This review critically examines advances in modified direct shear apparatuses for investigating soil–structure interfaces, including suction-control techniques based on axis translation and vapor equilibrium, surface-roughness modifications using smooth, grooved, and textured plates, dual-sided configurations, environmental controls, and thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) adaptations. Experimental findings from natural and artificial soils are synthesized to assess the effects of roughness, drainage, water content, normal stress, matric suction, and temperature on interface shear resistance. Particular attention is given to reported links between peak interface shear resistance and crack initiation in thin-layer desiccation tests, as well as the role of soil–water retention curves in interpreting suction-dependent behavior. Crack initiation mechanisms and THM studies on energy geostructures are discussed. Research gaps include multiscale coupling, testing standardization, and field validation. The review highlights the potential of accessible apparatus modifications to improve interface characterization and predictive modeling under variable climatic conditions.

papers.summary: Sustainable nutrient management is essential for agricultural productivity and soil function, yet short-term responses to fertilizer sources in horticultural systems remain poorly understood. This study evaluated how organic and inorganic fertilizers influence soil properties and tomato (Solanum lycopersicum L.) productivity over two growing seasons (2024–2025). A field experiment on a Crider silt loam soil at Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY, compared inorganic fertilizer, organic fertilizer, and an unfertilized control in a randomized complete block design with three replications. The inorganic fertilizer treatment consisted of NPK 6-24-24 and 34-0-0, while the organic fertilizer treatment consisted of a commercial dry granular organic fertilizer (NPK 4-6-3) composed of alfalfa, feather, bone, and fishbone meals, potassium sulfate, and kelp; both were broadcast at transplanting at rates meeting the soil-test N recommendation. Soil organic matter (OM) exhibited a depth × sampling time interaction in 2024 (p = 0.01), with post-harvest surface stratification diminishing by 2025. A treatment × depth interaction in 2025 (p = 0.01) showed both fertilizers increased OM only in the 0–5 cm layer. Total nitrogen increased under inorganic fertilizer in 2024 and under both fertilizer treatments in the surface layer in 2025. Soil bulk density, total porosity, and saturated hydraulic conductivity were not affected by the fertilizer source. Tomato fruit yield did not differ among the treatments in 2024 (77.7–85.9 t ha−1), whereas in 2025 it increased under inorganic fertilizer (66.6 t ha−1) and organic fertilizer (57.2 t ha−1) compared to the control (34.5 t ha−1). Overall, organic fertilizer achieved productivity comparable to inorganic fertilizer within two years, with increased surface OM and nitrogen, while soil physical properties remained unchanged.

papers.summary: Soil hydraulic properties (SHP), defined by the water retention curve (WRC) and the hydraulic conductivity curve (HCC), are crucial to describe water storage and flow in soils. Several methods have been developed and combined to measure these two fundamental curves across the full range from saturation to oven-dryness. However, for the HCC, there is still a data gap for pressure heads between approximately −1 to −100 cm, which is expected to be strongly affected by soil structure. We present an experimental workflow in which the multistep flux (MSF) method is integrated into the well-established combination of methods for measuring SHP, namely the falling head method, the simplified evaporation method, and the dew point method, specially designed to be applied to the same sample. The MSF is an adaptive, direct measurement of the HCC based on applying series of steady-state water flows to a soil sample characterised by unit hydraulic gradient. Once near steady-state flow conditions is achieved, the sample is characterised by a constant pressure head, constant water content and constant unsaturated hydraulic conductivity which is equal to the applied flux. We tested the method for three different soil columns: a repacked sand with a very well-defined air-entry pressure head and two undisturbed silt loams. For the sand, the MSF results coincide with the saturated hydraulic conductivity value, measured with the falling head method. For the undisturbed loam samples, the structural effect on the HCC is clearly visible. Integrating the MSF into the common lab-workflow to characterise SHP will help future studies to investigate soil structure effect on SHP.

papers.summary: Landslide dams, formed when landslide debris blocks a river, occur across Aotearoa New Zealand. These events pose serious hazards to downstream communities and infrastructure, as sudden breaches can result in unexpected flooding and debris flows. They are also important components of complex cascading slope-river systems. Despite their contribution to sediment cascades and potential flood hazard, they remain under-researched. Understanding the interactions between hydrological, geological, and climatic factors governing landslide dam evolution is crucial for hazard management planning. The Tairāwhiti Gisborne region on the East Coast of Aotearoa New Zealand is prone to landslides and subsequent dams, due to its steep slopes, susceptible lithology, and exposure to tropical storms from the east. Despite this vulnerability, very little is known about the material properties and behaviour of landslide dams in this area. The primary aim of this thesis was to investigate the geomorphic and geotechnical aspects of dams in the Tairāwhiti Gisborne region, to understand their formation and breach processes. papers.summary: Rainfall-induced slope instability is one of the most critical geotechnical hazards worldwide, causing significant damage to infrastructure and loss of life. Predicting slope stability under rainfall conditions remains challenging due to the complex interaction between soil properties, slope geometry, and transient hydrological processes. This research addresses this challenge by developing a reliable and practical predictive framework that integrates experimental investigation, numerical modeling, and machine learning. The study was conducted in three sequential stages. First, geotechnical centrifuge tests were performed at the University of Western Ontario to investigate slope response under controlled rainfall conditions. A calibrated rainfall simulation system ensured uniform and repeatable rainfall application, while slope deformation and pore water pressures were monitored to understand failure mechanisms. Second, numerical simulations using SEEP/W and SLOPE/W were conducted to evaluate slope stability across a wide range of conditions, including different soil types (clay, silt, and sand), slope geometries, and rainfall scenarios. This process generated a comprehensive dataset of 21,438 cases. Finally, machine learning models, including Multiple Linear Regression, Random Forest, and Extra Trees, were developed to predict the factor of safety using seven input variables. The Extra Trees model showed the highest predictive accuracy and strong generalization capability, particularly under unseen slope geometries. The results also highlight the importance of including rainfall intensity and duration in predictive models. The developed model was implemented into a web-based early warning system capable of providing rapid predictions. This research contributes to improved hazard assessment and supports the development of practical tools for geotechnical risk mitigation.

papers.title: Base-level lowering rates control a landslide process transition in California's Franciscan mélange
papers.summary: California’s Franciscan mélange is well-known for hosting persistent, slow-moving earthflows, a landslide style favored by the unit’s significant local variability in shear strength (e.g. Medley, 2001; Kim et al., 2004; Roering et al., 2015). Big Sur’s mélange, however, is unusual: landslide mapping there reveals both recent (e.g. the 2017 Mud Creek landslide) and prehistoric rotational landslides on slopes that are unusually steep for this lithology. Because rotational landslides and earthflows pose markedly different hazards, understanding what drives the shift in failure style is critical for hazard assessment. Here we test the hypothesis that the rate of base-level lowering governs the transition between earthflow and rotational failure. papers.summary: Landslides are processes involving the downslope movement of soil and/or rock masses due to slope instability. Wonogiri Regency exhibits diverse topographic, rainfall, geological, land-use, and soil characteristics, resulting in varying levels of landslide susceptibility across the region. This study aims to analyze the spatial distribution of landslide susceptibility levels and their correspondence with actual landslide occurrences in Wonogiri Regency. A quantitative method was employed using a Geographic Information System (GIS) approach via the Weighted Overlay method. The parameters utilized included rainfall, slope gradient, geology, land use, and soil type. Validation results show that 57 occurrence points (67.06%) fall within the high susceptibility class, while 28 points (32.94%) fall within the moderate susceptibility class; no occurrence points were found in the low susceptibility class. These findings demonstrate that actual landslides occurred more frequently in areas classified as having high susceptibility compared to those with moderate susceptibility.

This disaster is caused by a combination of natural factors, such as high rainfall, slope gradients, soil types, and human activities that alter land use. This study aims to analyze the landslide susceptibility levels and identify mitigation efforts in Ile Ape Timur Subdistrict. This research employed a descriptive method with a Geographic Information System (GIS) approach. The data used included slope gradient maps, soil type maps, rainfall data, and land use maps, analyzed using a weighted overlay technique to produce a landslide susceptibility map. Primary data were collected through field observations, while secondary data were obtained from relevant agencies such as BPBD and PUPR of Lembata Regency. The results show that the landslide susceptibility levels in Ile Ape Timur are categorized into four classes: not susceptible (3,174 hectares), less susceptible (25 hectares), susceptible (718 hectares), and highly susceptible (6 hectares). The main factors influencing susceptibility are steep slopes, Andosols soil prone to erosion, and relatively high annual rainfall. Recommended mitigation efforts include structural approaches, such as terracing and the installation of early warning systems (EWS), as well as non-structural approaches, including community education and disaster simulations. This study is expected to serve as a basis for the government and local communities to implement effective landslide disaster mitigation measures, minimizing material losses and casualties.

papers.summary: Vegetation has been used for slope stabilization for centuries, with conventional measures like soil nails and piles serving to complement the root reinforcement. Vegetation contributes to reinforcement through mechanical reinforcement provided by the root, and hydro-mechanical effects associated with evapotranspiration. Despite decades of research, translating root reinforcement into engineering practice remains unclear because most studies focus on specific plant species rather than on mechanically meaningful root traits, limiting comparability and predictive capability. papers.title: Understanding the rainfall triggering post-fire debris flows in California
papers.summary: Post-fire debris flows (PFDFs) are a cascading hazard resulting from the interaction between intense rainfall and susceptible terrain altered by wildfire. These events have proven devastating in the past, damaging infrastructure and communities, particularly in California, where fire season in the warm months is closely followed by rainfall during the cool season. The expansion of wildfire occurrence, along with pronounced variability in terrain and climate across California, highlights the need to better understand the rainfall conditions associated with this hazard under both current and future climates. Consequently, this dissertation integrates multiple datasets and methods to characterize rainfall and atmospheric conditions associated with storms triggering post-fire debris flows, providing new insight into the rainfall environments, precipitation-system structure, predictive controls, and future changes in PFDF hazard across California. First, an inventory of PFDF is compiled and used to characterize rainfall conditions associated with event occurrence using nearby rain gauges, including storm duration, rainfall accumulation, antecedent rainfall, and short-duration peak intensity. Results show that rainfall triggering PFDFs in California occurs within diverse storm environments, from long, persistent, and wet cool-season storms to shorter and intense warm-season storms. papers.summary: Surface soil moisture (SSM) is a key environmental variable controlling water and energy fluxes at the land-atmosphere interface. As part of the water cycle, SSM influences infiltration, runoff, evapotranspiration and determines plant water availability. Its accurate monitoring is essential for early agricultural drought detection, hydrological modelling and climate change adaptation. Over the last decades, satellite-based approaches have become prominent to monitoring SSM, providing temporally and spatially continuous observations in near-real-time. In particular, the Sentinel-1 satellites, carrying C-band synthetic aperture radar, provide SSM retrievals at an unprecedented sub-kilometer resolution, distributed through the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service. Despite the potential of the operational Sentinel-1 SSM, the product shows limitations over dense vegetation and complex topography, limiting its applicability for environmental monitoring in these landscapes. papers.title: Development of an advanced computational approach for early warning and predictions of rainfall-induced slope failures
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides are among the most common natural hazards, threatening lives, homes, and infrastructure worldwide. This research develops a novel approach to predict landslides and provide early warning, even when field data are limited. The study creates advanced computer models that represent real soil conditions and simulate how slopes respond to heavy rainfall. These physics-based models are then combined with machine learning that learn continuously from monitoring data, allowing predictions to be updated and refined over time. By improving prediction accuracy, this research supports more effective landslide early warning systems and helps reduce damage and loss of life.

papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility is a condition that indicates the level of potential for an area to experience landslides which is influenced by factors such as slope gradient, rainfall, soil type, geology, and land use. This study aims to analyze landslide susceptibility for determining shelter points in Petungkriyono District, Pekalongan Regency using a GIS (Geographic Information System)-based overlay method with ArcGIS 10.8 software. The data used include landslide occurrence data, DEMNAS Indonesia, RBI Indonesia, rainfall in 2014–2025, land use in 2025, distribution of disaster mitigation shelters, soil type, and geology of Petungkriyono District. The results of the study indicate that the level of landslide susceptibility in Petungkriyono District is dominated by high class with an area of 6930.5 Ha or 84.58%, medium class with an area of 1228.3 Ha or 14.99%, and low class with an area of 34.9 Ha or 0.43%. In general, every village in Petungkriyono District is characterized by high landslide vulnerability. Curugmuncar Village is the most vulnerable area, with a high vulnerability percentage reaching 96.68%. Disaster mitigation shelters are divided into four types: government, education, health, and worship shelters. There are three government shelters, 14 education shelters, one health shelter, and 27 worship shelters spread across all villages in Petungkriyono District.

Roads interrupt these controls by compressing peat and blocking lateral groundwater flow, producing persistent changes in water-table position, oxygen exposure, solute movement, and decomposition. As road removal and peatland reclamation become more common, restoration must be guided by how disturbance continues to affect ecosystem function below ground, rather than only whether vegetation or surface hydrology appear to recover. papers.title: Effects of root architecture of different wheat cultivars on soil structure
papers.source: AMS Dottorato Institutional Doctoral Theses Repository (University of Bologna)
papers.summary: Plant roots play a crucial role in maintaining soil health by influencing physical structure and hydraulic properties. This study investigates relationships between root morphology of wheat genotypes and their impacts on soil structure and hydraulic characteristics. Using shovelomics, we characterized root systems of wheat cultivars (Paragon, Bologna) and landraces (Senatore-Cappelli, Watkins238) selected for contrasting root morphologies. X-ray computed tomography (CT) was applied to examine soil pore networks at cylinder and aggregate scales, while soil hydraulic properties were measured using Wind evaporation and dew point techniques. Results demonstrated significant genotype-driven differences in soil morphology and hydraulic functions. Structural analyses (Minkowski functionals, percolation theory) showed significant variability in bioporosity and pore connectivity among genotypes compared to bare soil. Senatore-Cappelli exhibited notably larger biopores (>1 mm diameter). Hydraulic characterization using a van Genuchten bimodal model revealed statistically significant differences in soil water retention curves and hydraulic conductivity among genotypes. Root traits, including total root length, branching frequency, lateral root length, and root diameter, significantly correlated with soil pore size distribution and hydraulic parameters. This analysis underscores the importance of root architecture in modulating soil structure and water dynamics, highlighting the potential of specific wheat genotypes to affect soil health, water retention, and agricultural sustainability.

papers.title: EFFECTS OF DOLOMITE AMENDMENTS ON PER- AND POLYFLUOROALKYL SUBSTANCES (PFAS) LEACHING IN AGRICULTURAL SOILS
papers.summary: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are often found in agricultural soils due to land application of biosolids, wastewater-derived materials, and atmospheric deposition. However, PFAS transport behavior in variably saturated agricultural soils remains poorly studied. This study evaluates PFAS mobility within unsaturated soil using both intact soil cores (diameter: 3 inches, referred to as large columns (LC)) and packed, homogeneous soil columns (diameter: 1 inch, referred to as small columns (SC)) under the presence and absence of dolomite, which was recently reported to be able to reduce PFAS mobility through adsorption. All columns were amended with a biosolid (Milorganite) and half of the large and small columns received a powdered dolomite amendment at the surface. Columns were subjected to episodic infiltration based on precipitation data from 2019, and the leachate was collected at the base of each column for PFAS analysis. Our results showed that (1) the leaching of PFAS was strongly dependent on the structure and properties of the PFAS, and (2) dolomite amendments could lower the leaching of PFAS. The findings from this research will improve our quantitative understanding of how PFAS move through agricultural soils and the potential risks associated with land application, as well as the design and implementation of science-based management practices and regulation frameworks.

papers.summary: Water infiltration dynamics in block cave mining are critical to understanding and managing inrush hazards that threaten mine safety and operational continuity. Primary water sources, groundwater aquifers, water-bearing faults, and surface water entering through the subsidence crater interact within the cave muck pile through preferential flow pathways that develop and evolve during mining. How that water then partitions within the broken ore column has received less attention. This research investigates the development and flow behaviour of these pathways using an integrated physical and numerical modelling approach. A conceptual model of a draw column is proposed and tested, characterized by central compressive plug flow zones (PFZ) bounded by finer-grained shear bands (SB1, SB2) that respond differently under unsaturated and saturated conditions. papers.title: Study on hydraulic conductivity behaviour with regard to soil characteristics in landfill performance
papers.summary: Municipal solid waste generation continues to increase in Malaysia, placing greater demands on landfill containment systems to effectively prevent leachate migration and protect groundwater resources. The engineering performance of compacted landfill liners depends largely on the hydraulic conductivity achieved after compaction, which is governed by the combined influence of soil physical properties and compaction behaviour. However, the hydraulic performance of landfill-sourced residual soils in Malaysia remains insufficiently understood, particularly regarding the interaction between soil characteristics and hydraulic conductivity under realistic moisture and loading conditions. papers.summary: (English) Ecohydrology provides a critical framework for understanding interactions between vegetation and the hydrological cycle, particularly in forested ecosystems that strongly regulate water fluxes and ecosystem resilience. In Mediterranean mountain regions, increasing climate variability and recurrent droughts place forests close to their hydraulic limits. Despite these mounting pressures, key uncertainties remain regarding how trees access, store, and utilize water across contrasting wetness conditions, and how these processes can be represented in ecohydrological models. This thesis investigates tree water uptake dynamics and their representation by integrating high temporal- and spatial-resolution field observations, stable water isotopes, and process-based modeling. The study was conducted in the Vallcebre Research Catchments (NE Spain), focusing on Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris L.). Field observations combined meteorological measurements, sap flow and stem diameter variations, soil water content and potential, groundwater levels, and weekly water stable isotopes sampling of precipitation, soil water, groundwater, and xylem water. papers.title: Time-Lapse 3D Electrical Resistivity Tomography to Resolve Preferential Flow Paths in a Forestry Hillslope supported by a Brilliant Blue Tracer
papers.summary: Understanding subsurface water movement, particularly preferential water flow, is critical for water resource management and predicting contaminant transport. However, traditional invasive methods like dye staining experiments are destructive and only provide static information. Consequently, this thesis investigates the effectiveness of 3D time-lapse electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) for monitoring infiltration dynamics on a forested hillslope in Lower Austria. A Brilliant Blue saline tracer was applied to a 0.8 × 0.8 m plot during a two-hour irrigation event. ERT measurements were collected at 7-minute intervals and processed using various inversion strategies to resolve resistivity changes over time. The resistivity data were then used to delineate preferential flow paths and estimate pore water velocities.The ERT monitoring successfully captured the decrease in resistivity, directly corresponding to the infiltration of the tracer.The wetting front migrated rapidly to a depth of 0.25 m within the first 45 minutes before slowing to a maximum of 0.28 m at the end of the irrigation. Pore water velocities, derived from resistivity breakthrough curves, varied from 0.0002 cm/min in the soil matrix to up to 6 cm/min in localized preferential flow paths. Comparison of the ERT inversion results with the post-excavation Brilliant Blue staining patterns confirmed that the centers of conductive anomalies align with the staining patterns, although discrete macropores and root channels could not beresolved due to the limited resolution of the method.These results demonstrate that 3D time-lapse ERT is a robust, non-invasive tool for quantifying the spatio-temporal dynamics of preferential flow, though its resolution remains constrained by the electrode array geometry and the inherent smoothing of the inversion process.

However, the scientific valida-tion of such techniques is often caught up in disciplinary fragmentation and by the lack of long-term monitoring protocols capable of assessing both the evolution of slope stability and the success of environmental recovery.
