papers.title: Infiltration in a novel unsaturated multi-layered cover system for use in tailings storage facilities
papers.summary: Conventional barrier systems in tailings storage facilities often rely on thick monolithic geomaterials (1.5 m-2.5 m) or geosynthetics that fail under ex-treme precipitation or snowmelt events typical in Nordic climates. This study proposes and evaluates a novel, fully unsaturated multi-layered cover system (MLCS) constructed majorly from on-site sourced tailings and waste rock. The tailings are modified through either mixing with biochar and clay or by altering surface polarity to make them functional components of a newly conceptual-ized MLCS. The MLCS design integrates capillary barrier mechanisms with a water-entry-head-controlled hydrophobic interface to act as a final hydraulic buffer during extreme ponding conditions. Laboratory characterization of soil-water retention curves (SWRCs), unsaturated hydraulic conductivity functions (SHCFs), and hydrophobicity confirmed the enhanced water-buffering capaci-ty of the modified tailings mixtures. Especially, the threshold-based break-through resistance of the hydrophobic layer (WEH ≈ 4.71 kPa) allowed the construction of an overall thin MLCS (≤0.5-m-thick). This MLCS was physically modelled in an instrumented 1-D column subjected to a ponding head equivalent to a 500-year rainfall event. Results showed complete suppression of percolation below the MLCS for 61 days of testing period, with the hydro-phobic layer preventing breakthrough even after upper layers neared saturation. Complementary two-stage finite element simulations, incorporating WEH-triggered hydraulic switching, accurately reproduced observed suction, water-content, and percolation behaviour. The findings demonstrate that the proposed MLCS provides a climate-resilient, all-weather hydraulic barrier, reduces dependence on imported materials, and offers a feasible, low-cost closure strategy for Nordic TSFs. Further work should assess performance under field-scale slopes including lateral drainage conditions.

papers.title: Hydromechanical behaviour of unsaturated tailings: strength, brittleness, and fabric effects on water retention
papers.summary: This thesis investigates the hydromechanical behaviour of unsaturated tailings, specifically how fabric, saturation, and material type influence stability. Testing four distinct tailings materials revealed that void ratio, more than fabric, governs water retention. A critical saturation threshold of approximately 60–65% was identified for brittle failure in sandy silt tailings. The study indicates that saturation history alters mechanical response, with wetting after consolidation increasing brittleness. Constant volume DSS testing proved unconservative for unsaturated soils predicting saturated behaviour. Findings highlight that unlike sandy materials, clayey tailings undergo rapid suction collapse during undrained shear, which have implications for tailings storage facilities stability.

papers.title: Application of the Material Point Method to the Stability and Runout Analysis of Vegetated Slopes
papers.summary: Slope failures cause severe human and economic losses worldwide, yet conventional stability methods describe them only up to the onset of failure. Limit equilibrium methods treat the failing mass as rigid and perfectly plastic, and the finite element method is restricted to small deformations, so neither follows the slide once it forms. The Material Point Method (MPM) avoids this limitation by discretizing soil into Lagrangian material points that move through a fixed background mesh, so no mesh distortion develops under large deformation. This dissertation applies MPM to the analysis of slope failures in two parts, the assessment of slope stability and the influence of vegetation on rainfall-induced failures. The one-phase and coupled two-phase formulations are first derived and verified against classical benchmark problems in poromechanics. Next, MPM is applied to evaluate the stability of slopes using the strength reduction technique. For dry and unsaturated slopes, slip surfaces agree with finite element solutions and factors of safety differ by less than about 10%, reflecting the different criteria by which each method identifies failure. Unlike mesh-based methods, MPM continues past the onset of failure and captures the post-failure runout. The effect of root reinforcement is then investigated. A multiple-hardening constitutive model for root-reinforced soil is implemented within the coupled formulation and validated against triaxial tests. Comparative analyses of bare and vegetated slopes under rainfall show that roots delay the initiation of failure, roughly halve the displacement, and change a retrogressive slide into the movement of a single block, although they do not prevent failure under continued rainfall. Finally, the method is validated against a documented centrifuge slope test. papers.title: Development of Fracture Based Geotechnical Design of Clay Barriers
papers.summary: Compacted clay barriers are central components of landfill liners and covers, clay cores in embankment dams and tailings facilities, and other geoenvironmental containment systems. Their design is traditionally governed by classification, plasticity, compaction, hydraulic conductivity, shear strength, compressibility, and construction-quality requirements. These criteria are essential, but they do not directly measure the resistance of a compacted clay barrier to the initiation and extension of open-mode discontinuities and the subsequent formation of connected preferential flow paths. This omission is critical because an intact clay layer may meet the required low hydraulic conductivity, whereas the same layer can lose containment capacity when tensile cracks develop due to desiccation, differential settlement, shrinkage, hydraulic loading, or construction-induced fabric defects. The problem is particularly consequential for persistent contaminants such as per-and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), where landfill leachate can migrate through a liner with an open discontinuity, creating long-term exposure pathways to groundwater. The present study develops a fracture based geotechnical design framework for compacted clay barriers by combining laboratory fracture testing, effective single edge notched beam (SENB) calibration, state-dependent geotechnical characterization, numerical comparison of crack-propagation formulations with selected experimental measures, and sequential one-way fracture-to-flow modelling. papers.title: STUDI PERENCANAAN JALAN DAN PENGAMANAN LERENG PADA TRASE JALAN UJAN MAS PADA STA 0+050 SAMPAI STA 2+550
papers.summary: The development of safe and efficient road infrastructure is a crucial element in regional development. This study aims to conduct technical planning for new roads and slope protection systems on the Ujan Mas Road Trace (STA 0+050 to STA 2+550). Given the location's topography, which is dominated by steep slopes, this planning integrates geometric design of the road, pavement structure, drainage system, and retaining wall design. The study methodology includes primary and secondary data collection, hydrological analysis for the design flood discharge calculation, and soil mechanics investigation to ensure the stability of the retaining wall structure against overturning, shearing, and dynamic earthquake loads (Mononobe-Okabe method). In addition to technical aspects, this study also includes the preparation of a Cost Budget Plan (RAB) to accurately estimate construction funding requirements based on the calculated work volume. The geometric design of the road refers to the Bina Marga standard, while the pavement analysis uses the Bina Marga method. The final results of this study are expected to provide a comprehensive and economical technical solution for road infrastructure development in the area, while prioritizing safety aspects and sustainable slope stability

papers.title: Boundary Influence in Truncated Groundwater Models: Reconstructing a Local-Scale MODFLOW Model from a Consultant-Developed Regional Model in the Monterey Subbasin
papers.summary: Regional groundwater models built by consultants contain valuable calibrated frameworks but are often too large and complex for repeated local-scale analysis. Rather than rebuilding an entirely new smaller model, this study truncates the existing consultant-built regional model of the Monterey Subbasin, preserving the original grid structure and parameter framework while reducing the active domain to a manageable size for planning-level use. A key finding is that boundary-condition representation exerted a dominant influence on simulated groundwater behavior within the truncated domain, highlighting that truncation is a structural decision that meaningfully affects how the model responds. Model performance was evaluated two ways. Alternative hydraulic conductivity fields derived from AEM resistivity data were used to assess how sensitive the reconstructed model was to changes in internal parameter structure. Transient injection simulations produced cumulative groundwater mounding that grew progressively over repeated seasonal cycles, confirming realistic aquifer behavior and demonstrating the model's value as a practical and transparent planning-level tool.
